Title: The dual effects of digitalization on SMEs: export gains and learning losses
Authors: Emanuel Gomes, David W. Lehman, Ferran Vendrell-Herrero
Abstract: Abstract Longstanding debates persist about the impact of new technologies on firms, particularly as it relates to internationalization. Some scholars suggest that digitalization will enhance the benefits of export activity by facilitating connections with partners and customers. Others, however, suggest that digitalization will simply fail to live up to the hype—or perhaps even worse. This debate is especially relevant for SMEs given that export activity is the primary route to global markets for such firms. We propose that digitalization will exert dual effects on SMEs: on the “bright” side, larger investments in digital technologies will lead to greater export activity (i.e., higher export sales); on the “dark” side, however, digitalization-induced export activity will generate fewer learning opportunities from export partners (i.e., smaller productivity gains). The proposed hypotheses were tested and supported using detailed firm-level panel data from 20,133 Portuguese firms from 2010 to 2019. Additional analyses and case studies corroborate the proposed mechanisms and point to hybrid approaches as one possible way to balance these dual effects of digitalization. Taken together, the findings shed new light on the debate about the role of digitalization in internationalization efforts.

Title: Diversifying for resilience: how supply base international diversification relates to supply base sustainability performance
Authors: Palitha Konara, Alex Mohr, Vikrant Shirodkar, Valentin Kiefner
Abstract: Abstract Recent work in international business views supply base international diversification (SBID) as an important strategy for strengthening multinational enterprises’ (MNEs’) resilience to country-level disruptions. However, it remains unclear how this resilience-oriented strategy relates to MNEs’ parallel efforts to improve supply base sustainability performance (SBSP). Drawing on transaction cost economics and the literature on supply chain governance, we argue that increasing SBID lowers MNEs’ costs of switching away from suppliers with poor sustainability performance, while simultaneously raising the costs of monitoring sustainability across heterogeneous supplier-country contexts. Together, these countervailing mechanisms suggest an inverted U-shaped relationship between SBID and SBSP. We further argue that this relationship is moderated by an MNE’s own sustainability performance, its relational embeddedness with its suppliers, and the institutional distance between its home country and supplier countries. Our analyses of 320 U.S. firms listed in the S&P 500 over the period 2010–2019 support our hypotheses. Our findings highlight the tension that MNEs face in simultaneously enhancing the resilience and sustainability performance of their supply base and indicate that SBID should be optimized rather than maximized to balance these dual objectives.

Title: Correction: Moving beyond entry modes: toward a new paradigm of international involvement in an era of digitalization and global transitions
Authors: Noman Shaheer, Sali Li, Liang Chen, Keith D. Brouthers, Dan Li, Peter Liesch

Title: Public institutions, governance capability, and platform internationalization: institutional substitution at home and abroad
Abstract: Abstract Digital platforms often expand internationally faster than public institutions can evolve, raising the question of how they sustain operations in weak institutional environments. I theorize governance capability, defined as the firm-level ability to design, implement, and enforce rules regulating participant behavior, as a dual institutional substitute. When home-country institutions are weak, platforms develop governance capability to fill domestic institutional voids (substitution at home), establishing order and trust where public enforcement is limited. Once developed, this capability becomes transferable across borders, enabling platforms to navigate weak host-country institutions during internationalization (substitution abroad). Its effect is conditional: it is stronger when home country institutions are stronger than those of the host country, and for broker platforms whose governance routines can be replicated globally at lower cost. Using a longitudinal sample of 50 digital platforms from China and the United States entering 61 host countries between 1996 and 2023, I find support for these predictions. These results position governance capability as a portable institutional infrastructure, offering a capability-based alternative to structural responses such as diversification in institutionally weak contexts, and highlighting its role as a supply-side driver of platform internationalization that complements demand-side forces such as network effects.

Title: National identity rhetoric under bilateral geopolitical tensions: evidence from Taiwanese MNEs
Authors: Jin-Su Kang, Sunghoon Kim, Chuan-Kai Lee
Abstract: Abstract When geopolitical tensions pit home and host audiences against each other, how do multinational enterprises (MNEs) respond? We examine MNEs’ organizational identity work directed at external audiences under bilateral geopolitical tensions, where efforts to gain acceptance from one side may provoke backlash from the other. Focusing on MNEs’ national identity rhetoric—how firms use language to emphasize or downplay national affiliation—we analyze longitudinal data (2001–2020) from the public communications of two Taiwan-originated MNEs, Foxconn and TSMC, which operate amid the geopolitical dynamics of the Taiwan Strait. Our analysis identifies four rhetorical strategies—augmenting-localizing, augmenting-globalizing, ambiguating, and affirming—through which MNEs manage tensions associated with the expression of national affiliation. We theorize how the deployment of these strategies varies according to two key contingencies: the level of bilateral geopolitical tension and the MNE’s resource dependence on the host economy. We find that rising geopolitical tensions increase pressure on firms to actively calibrate their home identity, while host-country resource dependence shapes the extent to which firms accommodate host audiences. By highlighting rhetoric as a mechanism through which MNEs strategically manage national identity, this research contributes to the literature on MNEs’ responses to increasingly polarized geopolitical environments.

Title: Correction: The world is your office: how work from anywhere boosts talent, productivity and innovation
Governing cross-border innovation: how country-specific director experience enables board-level boundary spanning in MNEs
Authors: Pankaj Kumar, Felipe Calvano, Karen Schnatterly
Abstract: Abstract The internationalization of innovation is critical for multinational enterprises (MNEs), yet foreign subsidiaries often struggle to gain headquarters support for their innovations, while knowledge from subsidiary-country contexts remains underused in headquarters’ R&D. This study examines how directors with professional experience in a subsidiary country help boards govern these challenges. Drawing on boundary-spanning theory, we argue that such directors improve headquarters’ evaluation of subsidiary innovations and expand the scope of knowledge that headquarters draws upon. Using 8,264 firm-country-year observations for U.S.-headquartered MNEs from 2000 to 2021, we find that headquarters-based directors with experience in subsidiary countries are positively associated with both subsidiary innovations patented in the home market and headquarters’ use of subsidiary–country knowledge reflected in patent citations. Both relationships are amplified by knowledge distance, the divergence between home and subsidiary-country innovation systems, because directors are most consequential when headquarters’ cognitive frameworks are most misaligned with the subsidiary context. The findings contribute to international business, corporate governance, and innovation research by showing how board composition shapes where innovation is supported and which foreign knowledge enters headquarters-led R&D. Practically, MNEs can improve global innovation governance by matching directors’ international experience to the countries in which their subsidiaries operate.

Title: A conceptual model of acculturation from a dynamic person–environment fit perspective
Authors: Marcus A. Valenzuela, Yih-Teen Lee, Nana Yaa A. Gyamfi
Abstract: L'acculturation est un processus essentiel, mais insuffisamment théorisé, qui sous-tend l'adaptation interculturelle des expatriés et des migrants. Un postulat central dans la recherche sur l'acculturation est que l'adaptation dépend de l'adéquation entre les individus et leur environnement ; pourtant, le concept d'adéquation et son évolution dans le temps restent peu développés. Nous élaborons un modèle conceptuel dynamique de l'acculturation en intégrant la théorie de l'adéquation personne-environnement (P-E) à la recherche sur l'acculturation, et conceptualisons d’ailleurs l'acculturation comme une interaction continue entre les capacités et les besoins des individus, les exigences et les ressources de l'environnement, et la congruence des valeurs culturelles. Nous théorisons deux formes d'adéquation dans le processus d'acculturation: l'adéquation entre les exigences de l'environnement et les capacités de l'individu (demands-abilities) et l'adéquation entre les besoins de l'individu et les ressources offertes par l'environnement (needs-supplies). Ensemble, ces deux formes d'adéquation déterminent l'adaptation interculturelle et le stress acculturatif. Le modèle se déploie en trois phases : les conditions initiales d'acculturation définies par l'adéquation P-E et la congruence des valeurs; l'adaptation de l'adéquation déclenchée par le stress ; et l'alignement des valeurs à plus long terme. Dans ce cadre théorique, le stress acculturatif est reconceptualisé comme une force motivationnelle dont les effets dépendent du degré de congruence des valeurs et qui peut conduire à des réponses adaptatives ou inadaptées. Nous introduisons en outre des asymétries structurelles (sur-inadéquation versus sous-inadéquation) et temporelles (à court terme versus à long terme) afin d'expliquer comment les situations d'inadéquation génèrent des adaptations comportementales immédiates ainsi que des changements de valeurs à plus long terme. Ce modèle apporte une plus grande précision théorique pour comprendre les dynamiques de l’acculturation et fournit des pistes concrètes pour la gestion des professionnels en mobilité globale dans le contexte des affaires internationales. 文化适应是外派人员和移民的跨文化调适过程中的一个关键但尚未充分理论化的过程。文化适应研究的一个核心假设是，调适取决于个体与其环境之间的契合程度，但"契合"这一概念及其时间上的发展仍然未被充分探讨。我们通过将"人-环境契合"理论与文化适应研究相结合，提出了一个动态的文化适应概念模型，并将文化适应概念化为个体能力与需求、环境要求与供给以及文化价值观一致性之间的持续互动。我们提出了两种形式的文化适应契合——预期与表现契合（需求与能力）以及偏好与实现契合（需求与供给）——这两种契合共同塑造了跨文化调适和文化适应压力。该模型分三个阶段展开：由人—环境契合和价值观一致性所定义的初始文化适应条件；由压力触发的契合调适；以及更长期的价值观对齐。在这一框架下，文化适应压力被重新概念化为一种条件性的动机力量，可依价值观一致性的不同而驱动适应性或非适应性的反应。我们进一步引入结构性（契合过度与契合不足）与时间性（短期与长期）不对称性，以解释契合不良条件如何引发即时的行为调适以及更长期的价值观变化。该框架为理解文化适应动态提供了更高的理论精确性，并为在国际商业中管理全球流动的专业人士提供了切实可行的洞见。 Acculturation is a critical yet insufficiently theorized process underlying expatriates’ and migrants’ cross-cultural adjustment. A central assumption in acculturation research is that adjustment depends on the fit between individuals and their environment, yet the concept of fit and its temporal development remain underdeveloped. We develop a dynamic conceptual model of acculturation by integrating person–environment (P–E) fit theory with acculturation research, and conceptualize acculturation as a continuous interaction between individuals’ abilities and needs, environmental demands and supplies, and cultural value congruence. We theorize two forms of acculturation fit, expected–performed (demands–abilities) and preferred–enabled (needs–supplies), that jointly shape cross-cultural adjustment and acculturative stress. The model unfolds in three phases: initial acculturation conditions defined by P–E fit and value congruence; stress-triggered fit adaptation; and longer-term value alignment. Within this framework, acculturative stress is reconceptualized as a conditional motivational force that can drive adaptive or maladaptive responses depending on value congruence. Title: The green frontier: circular economy and firm resilience in multinational enterprises and internationally engaged firms
Authors: Ibrahim Shaheen, Francesco Devicienti, Alessandro Manello, Davide Vannoni
Abstract: Abstract This article examines whether circular economy (CE) strategies enhance firm resilience after systemic shocks. Building on the natural resource-based view, we argue that CE investments made before COVID-19 can strengthen resilience by converting sustainability-oriented capabilities into absorptive and adaptive capabilities. Yet this conversion is not automatic: it depends on firms’ ability to manage three tensions between efficiency and redundancy, continuity and reconfiguration, and strategic flexibility and coordinated commitment. We test these arguments using survey data on Italian firms matched with administrative financial records and estimate ordered probit models of post-shock recovery. The results show that pre-pandemic CE investments are positively associated with firm resilience. This relationship is strongest among multinational enterprises, weaker among other firms engaged in international activities, and not statistically significant among domestic firms. We also find that upstream CE strategies are more strongly associated with resilience than downstream strategies, particularly for multinational enterprises. Overall, the findings suggest that CE contributes to resilience when firms possess the organizational and international capabilities needed to govern, integrate, and reconfigure circular practices under disruption.

Title: Cross-border crowdfunding: an attention-based view
Authors: Supradeep Dutta, Yong Li, Christopher Courtney
Abstract: Abstract This study develops an attention-based view of cross-border crowdfunding by examining how informational cues in campaign narratives guide backers’ attention and funding decisions. Crowdfunding enables global reach but intensifies competition for limited backer attention. Extending the attention-based view from managerial attention in organizational settings to crowd attention on digital platforms, we conceptualize crowd attention as decentralized and stimulus-driven. We identify two key informational cues as attention stimuli: global narrative (universal relevance) and backer-country focus (localized engagement). We argue that these cues increase support for international campaigns but that their effects depend on campaign characteristics such as cultural orientation and market readiness, which align with different backer motives. We further propose that cultural differences amplify, rather than hinder, backers’ responsiveness to attention stimuli. Using large-scale Kickstarter data, we find support for our arguments and demonstrate how digital narratives shape attention and funding decisions in cross-border exchanges.

Title: Violent conflicts, institutional friction, and foreign divestment: the case of MNCs’ market exit from Russia
Authors: Dirk Holtbrügge, Marc Oberhauser, Laura Kirste
Abstract: Geopolitical conflicts can abruptly and significantly change the institutional conditions of multinational corporations (MNCs). Yet, the impact of such institutional friction on foreign divestment is not yet well understood. While prior research has conceptualized institutional friction as a dynamic alternative to static measures of institutional distance, its implications for firm behavior remain underexplored. We develop and test a model of institutional friction that captures how structural (political affinity), situational (military threat and regulatory responses), and operational (institutional embeddedness) friction jointly influence foreign divestment decisions, using the case of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Based on data from 864 MNCs operating in Russia, we find that institutional friction arising from political affinity and military threat, combined with firms’ institutional embeddedness, significantly affects exit decisions. In contrast, economic sanctions imposed by Western countries have no direct effect on MNCs’ exit decisions but become consequential through their interaction with other dimensions of institutional friction, amplifying the effects of political affinity and military threat. These findings advance international business research by providing a structured and empirically grounded framework for analyzing how geopolitical conflicts affect strategic responses of MNCs. Specifically, we demonstrate how structural, situational, and operational frictions shape MNCs’ market exit decisions. This article explores how multinational corporations (MNCs) decide to leave or stay in a foreign market during violent conflicts, using the Russian invasion of Ukraine as a case study. Traditionally, scholars have used the concept of "institutional distance" to explain these decisions, focusing on the differences between the home and host countries. However, this approach does not account for the dynamic nature of geopolitical events. The authors introduce the concept of "institutional friction," which considers the changing political, military, and regulatory conditions that affect MNCs' operations. The study aims to understand why some MNCs exited Russia after the invasion, while others stayed. This article develops a model of institutional friction, drawing an analogy to physical friction, which is the resistance encountered when two surfaces move against each other. The model identifies three types of friction: structural, situational, and operational. Structural friction relates to long-term political alignment between countries. Situational friction arises from immediate geopolitical events, like military threats or sanctions. Operational friction involves the MNC's level of integration in its home and host country and the subsidiary's role within the MNC. The study uses data from 864 MNCs to test how these frictions influence their decision to exit a market. The authors also examine the role of "organizational lubricants," such as local partnerships, which can reduce friction. The study finds that low political affinity and high military threat increase the likelihood that MNCs will exit a market. Sanctions alone do not directly cause exits but amplify existing frictions. The presence of local partners does not significantly reduce friction in high-intensity conflicts like the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The authors conclude that institutional friction provides a more dynamic and comprehensive framework for understanding MNCs' responses to geopolitical conflicts. This framework can help managers and policymakers anticipate and respond to such events. Future research could explore how different types of geopolitical conflicts affect MNCs and the role of organizational lubricants in various contexts. Title: The world is your office: how work from anywhere boosts talent, productivity and innovation
Multinational enterprises’ strategic responses to geopolitical tensions and sanctions
Authors: Rajeev J. Sawant, Abdul-Kadir Ameyaw, Len J. Treviño, Yuan Li
Abstract: Rising geopolitical tensions and concomitant sanctions significantly affect multinational enterprises’ (MNEs), yet the theory of MNEs’ strategic responses remains underdeveloped. Through a qualitative study using the Russia–Ukraine conflict as a natural experiment, we investigate how and why MNEs respond strategically to these complex conditions. MNEs recognize that these stigmatize the MNE subsidiary’s host country. Continued association with a stigmatized location leads to cross-border stigma translation risk that threatens the MNE’s network resources and non-location-bound firm-specific advantages (FSAs). While some MNEs divest to prevent cross-border stigma translation risk from tainting such resources and FSAs, others freeze operations or stay. Those who freeze operations mitigate cross-border stigma translation risk while preserving subsidiary resources to generate potential non-location-bound FSAs, labeled subsidiary-generated FSAs (SG-FSAs). We uncover two novel mechanisms enabling MNEs to stay while mitigating stigma risk: ‘downgrading non-location-bound FSAs’ achieved through resource transfer, isolation, and recombination processes, and ‘downgrading non-location-bound SG-FSA exploitation’ achieved by embedding SG-FSAs in products restricted to the host country. We develop a theoretical model of MNE responses to sanctions, explaining how MNEs manage cross-border stigma translation risks and why MNE strategic configurations drive MNE responses. Our study contributes to understanding how and why MNEs respond to sanctions from geopolitical tensions. O aumento das tensões geopolíticas e as sanções correspondentes afetam significativamente as empresas multinacionais (MNEs), mas a teoria sobre as respostas estratégicas dessas MNEs permanece subdesenvolvida. Por meio de um estudo qualitativo que utiliza o conflito Rússia-Ucrânia como experimento natural, investigamos como e por que MNEs respondem estrategicamente a essas condições complexas. MNEs reconhecem que essas condições estigmatizam o país anfitrião da subsidiária. A associação contínua a uma localização estigmatizada aumenta o risco de tradução do estigma transfronteiriço, que ameaça os recursos da rede da MNE e as vantagens específicas da empresa não vinculadas à localização (FSAs). Enquanto algumas MNEs desinvestem para evitar que o risco de tradução de estigma transfronteiriço contamine esses recursos e FSAs, outras congelam suas operações ou permanecem operando. Aquelas que congelam operações mitigam o risco de tradução do estigma transfronteiriço, enquanto preservam os recursos da subsidiária para gerar potenciais FSAs não vinculadas à localização, denominadas FSAs geradas pela subsidiária (SG-FSAs). Descobrimos dois mecanismos inovadores que permitem que MNEs permaneçam enquanto mitigam o risco de estigma: “redução das FSAs não vinculadas à localização”, alcançada por meio de processos de transferência, isolamento e recombinação de recursos, e “redução da exploração de SG-FSAs não vinculadas à localização”, alcançada por meio da incorporação de SG-FSAs em produtos restritos ao país anfitrião. Desenvolvemos um modelo teórico das respostas de MNEs às sanções, explicando como as MNEs gerenciam os riscos de tradução de estigma transfronteiriço e por que as configurações estratégicas das MNEs impulsionam suas respostas. Nosso estudo contribui para a compreensão de como e por que MNEs respondem às sanções decorrentes de tensões geopolíticas. The article explores how and why multinational enterprises (MNEs) respond to geopolitical tensions and international sanctions. While previous research has primarily examined the macroeconomic impacts of geopolitical tensions, this study aims to understand why MNEs choose different strategic responses, such as divesting, freezing operations, or continuing operations, despite facing the same geopolitical shock. Title: The uneven path to global value chain upgrading: regulations, private governance, and supplier compliance
Authors: Shubham Singh, Ajai Gaur, Ram Mudambi
Abstract: Abstract Global value chains (GVCs) generate efficiency through production fragmentation but simultaneously create sustainability vulnerabilities that can undermine GVC resilience. While MNE buyer-led private ordering and state regulation represent the primary governance responses to these risks, their effects on supplier compliance remain contested. We develop a domain-sensitive governance framework showing that labor and environmental compliance differ systematically in their cost–benefit structures, and which in turn shape the effectiveness of governance forms in driving compliance across sustainability domains. Using a panel of over 2000 suppliers across emerging economies, we find evidence for the asymmetric effectiveness of governance forms across compliance domains. In the labor domain, both regulation and private ordering improve compliance, as stronger labor regulations increase MNE sourcing and reinforce suppliers’ incentives to upgrade. In contrast, in the environmental domain, while private ordering improves compliance, stringent environmental regulation reduces MNE sourcing, weakening suppliers’ incentives to invest in environmental improvements. We identify a buyer–regulation intermediation mechanism through which regulatory stringency shapes supplier compliance indirectly by altering MNE sourcing strategies. Our findings advance GVC governance research by showing that sustainability compliance, and thus resilience, depends not only on governance instruments but also on domain-specific incentive structures and buyer-mediated governance dynamics.

Title: Business and management research on societal wellbeing: a historic, multi-journal and large language model analysis of the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals
Authors: Farzam Boroomand, Anne S. Tsui, Ibrat Djabbarov, Arjen van Witteloostuijn, Wilfred Mijnhardt
Abstract: Les 17 Objectifs de Développement Durable des Nations Unies fournissent un cadre pour catégoriser les recherches qui abordent les défis mondiaux et font progresser le bien-être sociétal. En utilisant plusieurs grands modèles de langage, cette recherche a analysé 47197 articles publiés dans 18 revues de commerce et de gestion, y compris le Journal of International Business Studies , représentant cinq disciplines de commerce et de gestion sur une période de 55 ans (1970-2024). L'objectif était d'évaluer dans quelle mesure les chercheurs, y compris ceux en affaires internationales ( International Business ), s'attaquent aux problématiques liées aux grands défis tels que définis par les 17 Objectifs de Développement Durable des Nations Unies. Les résultats montrent que parmi les 47197 articles, 17,4 % sont liés à un ou plusieurs ODD. Ce pourcentage a augmenté au fil du temps, passant de 8 % avant l'introduction de l'Agenda 21 des Nations Unies en 1992 à 31 % après le lancement de l'Agenda 2030 de ces dernières en 2015. Les ODD 8 (Travail Décent et Croissance Economique), 9 (Industrie, Innovation et Infrastructure) et 16 (Paix, Justice et Institutions Efficaces) représentent 78 % des articles alignés sur les ODD. Le JIBS figure parmi les revues les plus influentes contribuant à ces ODD. Nous proposons des suggestions sur la manière dont la recherche en IB peut contribuer au bien-être sociétal en accordant davantage d'attention aux complémentarités entre les objectifs et en explorant les compromis où les progrès sur un objectif peuvent freiner l'avancement sur un autre. 联合国的17项可持续发展目标 (SDG) 为应对全球挑战和促进社会福祉的研究分类提供了框架。通过使用多个大型语言模型， 本研究分析了在18本商业与管理期刊 (包括《国际商业研究杂志》) 上发表的47,197篇文章， 涵盖了五个商业与管理学科， 时间跨度为55年（1970-2024年）。目标是评估包括国际商业（IB）学者在内的学者们在多大程度上解决了与联合国17项可持续发展目标所体现的重大挑战相关的问题。 研究结果显示， 在47,197篇文章中， 有17.4%与一个或多个SDG相关。这个比例随着时间的推移而增加， 从1992年联合国《21世纪议程》发布之前的8%上升到2015年联合国《2030议程》推出后的31%。在这些与SDG相关的文章中， SDG8（体面工作和经济增长）、SDG9（产业、创新和基础设施）以及SDG16（和平、正义与强大制度）占据了78%的比例。《国际商业研究杂志》(JIBS) 是对这些SDG做出贡献的领先期刊之一。我们就IB研究如何通过更加关注目标之间的互补性以及探索权衡 (一个目标的进步可能会阻碍另一个目标的进展)为社会福祉做出贡献提出了一些建议。 The United Nations’ 17 Sustainable Development Goals provide a framework for categorizing research that addresses global challenges and advances societal wellbeing. Using multiple large language models, this study analyzed 47,197 articles published in 18 business and management journals, including the Journal of International Business Studies , representing five business and management disciplines over 55 years (1970–2024). The objective was to assess the extent to which scholars, including those in IB, are tackling issues related to grand challenges as captured by the United Nation’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals. Findings show that among the 47,197 articles, 17.4% relate to one or more SDGs. This percentage increased over time, from 8% before the introduction of UN Agenda 21 in 1992 to 31% after the launch of UN Agenda 2030 in 2015. SDGs 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) accounted for 78% of the SDG-aligned articles. The JIBS is among the leading journals contributing to these SDGs. We offer suggestions on how IB research can contribute to societal wellbeing by paying more attention to complementarities among goals and exploration of trade-offs where progress on one goal may impede advancement on another. Title: Tax avoidance and ESG disclosure mandates: international evidence
Authors: Sadok El Ghoul, Omrane Guedhami, Yongtae Kim, Hyo Jin Yoon
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines how regulations mandating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure affect corporate tax behavior. Using a difference-in-differences analysis on a sample of firms from 48 countries, we find that ESG disclosure mandates lead to significant reductions in tax avoidance, with stronger effects for mandates that include tax-relevant provisions. We identify increases in ESG information transparency and improvements in firms’ ESG performance as channels through which ESG disclosure mandates reduce tax avoidance. We further find that the decrease in tax avoidance following ESG disclosure mandates is more pronounced in countries with weaker financial disclosure requirements, legal and tax enforcement, and environmental and social institutions. Collectively, the evidence suggests that non-financial disclosure regulations can curb aggressive tax behavior, supporting broader goals of corporate accountability and sustainable development.

Title: Impact investment as an enabler of firm formalization in the Global South
Authors: Gilbert Kofi Adarkwah, Peter Kalum Schou
Abstract: We examine whether and how impact investment—investing to secure both financial and social returns—is associated with formalization at founding. While impact investing has increasingly been promoted as a tool to support economic development, evidence on its relationship with patterns of formal firm entry in the Global South remains limited. This is important because while informality provides important livelihoods, widespread informal activity constrains growth, limits employment quality, and weakens public revenue generation, thereby hindering broader economic development. Building on the external enabler framework, we theorize that impact investment increases the likelihood that new firms register formally at inception. This relationship operates through two pathways: directly, by improving access to resources and enhancing the viability and legitimacy of formal operations; indirectly, by reducing corruption. Analyzing a novel, comprehensive dataset of impact investments in 86 countries, we find support for our hypotheses. These effects are particularly strong in lower-middle-income countries, illustrating the varying effects of impact investment. By providing large-scale, cross-country evidence on how impact investors affect new-firm formalization, we advance work on firm formalization and external enablement. In many parts of the Global South, many businesses operate informally, meaning they are not registered with the government. This can limit their growth and the overall economic potential of a country. Informal businesses often struggle with legitimacy, access to finance, and the ability to attract skilled employees. They also do not pay taxes, which affects public services. Impact investing, which aims to achieve social outcomes alongside financial returns, is proposed as a way to encourage businesses to formalize. This study explores whether impact investing can help businesses in the Global South formalize and how it might do so. This article analyzes data from 15 European firms investing in 86 countries in the Global South. The study uses the external enabler framework, which looks at how changes in the business environment can help firms. The researchers argue that impact investing can help businesses formalize by providing resources, increasing demand, and enhancing legitimacy. It can also reduce corruption, which is a major barrier to formalization. Corruption involves public officials demanding bribes, which increases the cost and risk of formalizing a business. Impact investors often have anti-corruption policies and can influence local practices by refusing to pay bribes and promoting transparency. The study finds that impact investing is associated with a higher likelihood of businesses formalizing at their inception. It shows that impact investing can reduce corruption, making it easier for businesses to operate formally. The research highlights that impact investing is most effective in countries with some level of institutional development, but not in very low or high-income countries. The findings suggest that impact investing can play a significant role in encouraging formal business operations, which can lead to better economic outcomes. Future research could explore more detailed data on how impact investments affect specific regions and sectors. Title: Method-driven theory advancements and AI implementation
Bond market liberalization and corporate investment
Authors: Renhui Fu, Fang Gao, Yanhui Wang, Bohui Zhang
Abstract: The article explores the impact of bond market liberalization on corporate investment, focusing on China's experience with the Bond Connect program. Bond Connect, launched in July 2017, allowed foreign investors to trade in China's interbank bond market, which was previously inaccessible to them. The study aims to fill the gap in understanding how opening bond markets to foreign investors affects corporate investment, as most research has focused on stock market liberalization. The key finding is that bond market liberalization leads to a decrease in corporate investment, particularly in overinvestment, which improves investment efficiency. This article uses a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to compare firms affected by Bond Connect (treatment group) with those that were not (control group). The treatment group consists of firms issuing bonds in the China Interbank Bond Market (CIBM), while the control group includes firms issuing bonds only in the China Exchange Bond Market (CEBM). The study uses data from 2013 to the fourth quarter of 2021, covering periods before and after the launch of Bond Connect. The DID method helps isolate the effect of bond market liberalization by controlling for other factors that might influence investment. The study also employs propensity score matching to ensure that the treatment and control groups are comparable. The results show that bond market liberalization reduces capital expenditure by firms, supporting the hypothesis that foreign bondholders impose more restrictive covenants, leading to less aggressive investment strategies. The study identifies three channels through which foreign investors influence investment: restrictive covenants, reputational costs, and litigation risks. Firms with higher exposure to foreign investors tend to include more covenants in their bond contracts, face higher reputational costs, and are more cautious due to potential litigation risks. These factors collectively lead to a reduction in overinvestment, thereby improving investment efficiency. In conclusion, the study demonstrates that bond market liberalization can enhance corporate governance by curbing inefficient investments. This finding contrasts with the common belief that liberalization leads to increased risk-taking. The research contributes to the literature by highlighting the governance role of foreign debtholders, who influence corporate behavior through non-ownership mechanisms. The study's insights have policy implications, suggesting that opening bond markets to foreign investors can complement domestic governance structures, especially in emerging markets like China. Future research could explore the long-term effects of bond market liberalization on economic growth and financial stability. Title: Resilience duality in global turbulence: immunity and growth
Hypothesis-testing research in international business: progress, pitfalls, and a way forward
Authors: Jelena Cerar, B. Sebastian Reiche, Phillip C. Nell
Abstract: Abstract Building on Meyer, van Witteloostuijn, and B eugelsdijk’s (2017) editorial on best practices for conducting and reporting hypothesis-testing research in IB, we examine the extent to which their guidelines—and related recommendations by Hahn and Ang (2017)—have been adopted in leading IB journals. We analyze all null-hypothesis significance testing-based articles published in the Journal of International Business Studies and the Journal of World Business between 2012 and 2024, using fine-grained inferential trend analyses of methodological and reporting standards alongside state-of-the-art tests for p-hacking and publication bias. Our results indicate meaningful progress in several areas, including greater methodological rigor and transparency. However, adoption remains uneven and has plateaued for several practices. Persistent shortcomings include limited reporting of standard errors, confidence intervals, and effect sizes, incomplete disclosure of robustness analyses and outlier treatment, and the continued predominance of confirmed hypotheses. Moreover, we find no evidence that p-hacking or publication bias have declined over time. Drawing on these results, we outline actionable recommendations for advancing methodological and reporting standards in IB by (1) enhancing transparent reporting, (2) providing convincing evidence, and (3) reporting and probing null and negative results. Overall, our study offers a roadmap for strengthening research credibility in IB.

Title: The impact of the global minimum tax on incentives for business location, investment, and profit shifting
Authors: François Bares, Michael P. Devereux, İrem Güçeri, Vikram Patil
Abstract: Abstract In 2021, over 140 countries agreed to what is widely considered to be the most significant reform of international business taxes in a century: the introduction of a global minimum tax (GMT) at a rate of 15% on the profits of large MNEs. We study the reform’s impact on three interrelated MNE decisions: the location of investment, the size of investment conditional on location, and the extent to which profit is shifted to a low-tax country. We extend existing models of the impact of taxation on investment incentives to allow for profit shifting and the GMT. We also develop and quantify a measure of the economic cost of tax-induced distortions to location. We apply our model to taxes in 34 OECD countries. Raising the GMT rate reduces profit shifting as the benefits of profit shifting are reduced. This raises the MNE’s tax liability and its cost of capital, reducing its aggregate investment. The impact on location choice is more subtle, as the dispersion in effective tax rates across countries first rises, then falls, as the GMT rate rises. At a GMT rate of 15%, we estimate that there is a small rise in the dispersion, implying greater distortions to location decisions.

Title: Spillover effects of cross-border bank acquisitions on systemic risk
Abstract: Usando una muestra de 639 adquisiciones bancarias transfronterizas en 65 países entre 1995 y 2019, examinamos los efectos de contagio de dichas adquisiciones sobre el riesgo sistémico de los bancos no objetivos (pares) en los países anfitriones. Encontramos que las adquisiciones bancarias transfronterizas conducen a un aumento en el riesgo sistémico de los bancos pares. Evaluamos hipótesis contrapuestas relacionadas con factores institucionales moderadores y con los canales subyacentes en funcionamiento. Nuestros hallazgos muestran que las adquisiciones bancarias transfronterizas reducen el poder de mercado y de fijación de precios de los bancos pares, lo que los lleva a orientarse hacia actividades de ingresos no financieros más volátiles. Este cambio hacia actividades basadas en comisiones, que tienden a ser más cíclicas y requieren menos capital, genera un aumento en el riesgo sistémico. Encontramos poca evidencia de que estén en funcionamiento canales relacionados con el riesgo crediticio o con choques de financiamiento. Los efectos adversos de contagio se mitigan en los países anfitriones donde los bancos pares probablemente disfruten de ventajas informativas en comparación con los nuevos entrantes extranjeros debido a una mayor liability of foreignness (desventaja de extranjería). En particular, los efectos de contagio se reducen para los bancos pares en países anfitriones con una cultura menos abierta y confiada hacia los extranjeros, y en países con una supervisión bancaria más estricta. Nuestros hallazgos contribuyen al debate en curso sobre los beneficios y costos de la globalización bancaria. Usando uma amostra de 639 aquisições bancárias transfronteiriças em 65 países no período de 1995 a 2019, examinamos os efeitos de transbordamento dessas aquisições sobre o risco sistêmico de bancos não-alvo (pares) nos países anfitriões. Descobrimos que aquisições bancárias transfronteiriças levam a aumentos no risco sistêmico dos bancos pares. Avaliamos hipóteses concorrentes relacionadas a fatores institucionais moderadores e a canais subjacentes em funcionamento. Nossas descobertas mostram que as aquisições bancárias transfronteiriças reduzem o poder de mercado e de precificação dos bancos pares, levando-os a se deslocarem para atividades de receita não proveniente de juros, mais voláteis. A mudança para essas atividades tarifárias, que tendem a ser mais cíclicas e a exigir menos capital, resulta em um aumento do risco sistêmico. Encontramos poucas evidências de risco de crédito ou de que um canal de choque de financiamento esteja em operação. Os efeitos adversos do transbordamento são mitigados em países anfitriões, onde os bancos pares provavelmente desfrutam de vantagens informacionais em relação aos entrantes estrangeiros, devido à maior desvantagem de ser estrangeiro. Especificamente, os efeitos de transbordamento são mitigados em bancos pares em países anfitriões com uma cultura menos aberta e menos confiante em relação a estrangeiros, e em países com supervisão bancária mais rigorosa. Nossas descobertas contribuem para o debate em curso sobre os benefícios e custos da globalização bancária. 用1995至2019年间65个国家的639个跨境银行的并购样本, 我们研究了此类并购对东道国非目标 (同业) 银行系统性风险的溢出效应。我们发现, 跨境银行并购导致同业银行系统性风险增加。我们对涉及调节性制度因素和内在传导渠道的竞争性假设进行了评估。研究结果表明, 跨境银行并购降低了同业银行的市场与定价能力, 使它们转向波动性更高的非利息收入业务。向此类收费型业务的转移——这类业务往往具有更强的周期性且需较少的资本——导致系统性风险持续积累。我们几乎没有发现信用风险或资金冲击渠道发挥作用的证据。在同业银行相对于外资进入者可能享有信息优势的东道国中, 由于外来者劣势 (liability of foreignness) 较高, 这种不利的溢出效应有所缓解。具体而言, 在文化上对外国人较不开放和信任度较低的东道国, 以及银行监管较为严格的国家, 溢出效应会得到缓解。我们的研究结果为银行全球化利弊得失这一持续辩论做出了贡献。 Using a sample of 639 cross-border bank acquisitions in 65 countries from 1995 to 2019, we examine the spillover effects of such acquisitions on the systemic risk of non-target (peer) banks in host countries. We find that cross-border bank acquisitions lead to increases in peer banks’ systemic risk. Title: Offshoring’s hidden toll: mental distress among onshore employees
Authors: Robin John Clerckx, Christoph Grimpe, Bart Leten, Mark Vancauteren
Abstract: La délocalisation est une stratégie centrale par laquelle les entreprises réorganisent leurs opérations à l'échelle mondiale, mais on sait peu de choses sur ses conséquences imprévues en termes de détresse mentale chez les employés restés sur place. Nous appuyant sur la théorie transactionnelle du stress et la littérature de la délocalisation, nous théorisons que la délocalisation augmente la détresse mentale, car cet événement est perçu comme une menace difficile à gérer. Nous argumentons en outre que cet impact n'est pas uniforme, mais dépend de conditions qui amplifient le risque perçu de perte d'emploi ou limitent les opportunités de réemploi. Pour tester ces arguments, nous construisons un ensemble de données complet employeur-employé aux Pays-Bas, dans lequel la détresse mentale est mesurée à l'aide des prescriptions de médicaments psychotropes. Nos analyses révèlent que la délocalisation entraîne une augmentation substantielle de la probabilité de consommation de médicaments psychotropes chez les employés restés sur place, et ce, jusqu'à trois ans après l'événement. De plus, les impacts deviennent plus prononcés lorsque la délocalisation s'accompagne de licenciements et chez les travailleurs peu ou moyennement qualifiés, migrants et âgés. Ensemble, nos résultats mettent en évidence que la délocalisation engendre des coûts humains non négligeables et durables, en particulier pour les employés les plus vulnérables à ses conséquences. Pour les managers et les organisations, ces résultats soulignent que les initiatives de délocalisation nécessitent des efforts soutenus et ciblés pour atténuer la détresse mentale et garantir une mise en œuvre efficace. 离岸外包是企业重组其全球运营的核心战略， 然而离岸外包对在岸员工心理困扰的意外影响却知之甚少。将压力与应对的交易理论与离岸外包文献相结合， 我们提出理论认为， 离岸外包会加剧心理困扰， 因为这一事件被视为难以应对的威胁。我们进一步指出， 这种影响并非均一， 而是取决于能够放大感知的失业风险或限制再就业机会的特定条件。为了验证这些观点， 我们构建了一个来自荷兰的雇主-雇员综合数据集， 其中心理困扰通过精神类药物处方来衡量。我们的分析显示， 离岸外包显著增加了在岸员工使用精神类药物的可能性， 这一影响在事件发生后可持续长达三年。此外， 当离岸外包伴随裁员时， 以及在中低技能员工、移民员工和年长员工群体中， 这种影响尤为突出。综合来看， 我们的研究结果表明， 离岸外包带来了不可忽视且持久的人力成本， 尤其是对那些最容易受其影响的员工而言。对于管理者和组织而言， 这些结果强调了离岸外包举措需要持续且有针对性的努力， 以缓解心理困扰， 并确保有效实施。 La deslocalización internacional (offshoring en inglés) es una estrategia central mediante la cual las empresas reorganizan sus operaciones globales, pero se sabe poco sobre sus consecuencias no intencionadas en el distrés mental de los empleados en el país de origen. Integrando la Teoría Transaccional del Estrés y Afrontamiento con la literatura sobre deslocalización, teorizamos que la deslocalización eleva el distrésmental, ya que el evento se percibe como una amenaza difícil de afrontar. Además, argumentamos que el efecto no es uniforme, sino que depende de condiciones que amplifican el riesgo percibido de pérdida de empleo o limitan las oportunidades de reempleo. Para probar estos argumentos, construimos una base de datos comprehensiva de empleadores y empleados en los Países Bajos, en el cual el distrés mental se mide mediante las prescripciones de medicamentos psicotrópicos. Nuestros análisis revelan que la deslocalización conduce a un aumento sustancial en la probabilidad de uso de medicamentos psicotrópicos entre los empleados locales, que persiste hasta tres años después del evento. Además, los efectos se vuelven más pronunciados cuando la deslocalización va acompañada de despidos y entre trabajadores de baja y media cualificación, migrantes y empleados de mayor edad. En conjunto, nuestros hallazgos destacan que la deslocalización conlleva costos humanos de importancia real y duraderos, particularmente para los empleados más vulnerables a sus consecuencias. Para los gerentes y las organizaciones, estos resultados subrayan que las iniciativas de deslocalización requieren esfuerzos sostenidos y específicos para mitigar el distrés mental y garantizar una implementación efectiva. Title: Collectivist culture and corporate social responsibility
Authors: Xin Yu, Shijun Guo, Zhou Zhang
Abstract: Com base na teoria do arroz, que relaciona o cultivo de arroz a culturas coletivistas, investigamos se a cultura regional coletivista influencia a responsabilidade social corporativa (CSR). Descobrimos que empresas chinesas em regiões com culturas coletivistas mais fortes apresentam desempenho superior em CSR e realizam mais doações de caridade. Essa relação é robusta em diversas estratégias de identificação, incluindo um experimento quase-natural com base no terremoto de Sichuan de 2008 e uma análise de empresas localizadas ao longo da fronteira agrícola entre arroz e trigo. A análise dos mecanismos revela que o efeito positivo da cultura coletivista na CSR é mais evidente em empresas com laços locais mais estreitos ou sob maior escrutínio público, sugerindo que esse efeito opera principalmente por meio da pressão social e das expectativas dos stakeholders. Além disso, o engajamento em CSR mitiga os riscos corporativos de forma mais eficaz em regiões com culturas coletivistas mais fortes, indicando que a cultura local atua como um “multiplicador” do valor do seguro social da CSR. Nossas evidências transnacionais mostram ainda que tanto o coletivismo baseado no cultivo de arroz quanto as medidas convencionais de individualismo predizem positivamente os resultados de RSC, sugerindo que essas dimensões representam continuidades distintas, em vez de polos opostos. Essa descoberta ressalta a natureza híbrida da CSR, permitindo a convergência de diferentes caminhos culturais. For multinational enterprises, our findings highlight the importance of adapting CSR strategies to both national and subnational cultural contexts. Para empresas multinacionais, nossos achados destacam a importância de adaptar as estratégias de RSC aos contextos culturais tanto nacionais quanto subnacionais. This article explores how cultural factors, specifically collectivist culture, influence corporate social responsibility (CSR) practices. Companies are part of society and can create wealth but also cause negative effects like environmental harm. Legitimacy theory suggests that companies need to align with societal norms to be accepted. CSR is a way for companies to show they care about societal expectations. While formal rules are known to affect CSR, the role of informal cultural influences is less understood. This study examines how collectivist culture, which values group interests over individual ones, impacts CSR activities. The study uses China as a case because of its strong collectivist culture and employs the rice theory, which links rice farming to collectivism, to test its hypotheses. This article uses data from Chinese firms to investigate the relationship between collectivist culture and CSR. The rice theory suggests that rice farming, which requires cooperation, fosters collectivism, while wheat farming, which requires less cooperation, fosters individualism. The study focuses on firms in regions with different farming practices to see how these cultural differences affect CSR. The researchers use data from Chinese stock markets and statistical yearbooks to analyze CSR performance and charitable donations. They also examine how firms respond to external shocks, like the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, to understand the role of collectivism in CSR. The study uses regression models to analyze the data, controlling for various factors that might influence CSR. The study finds that firms in collectivist regions engage more in CSR and make more charitable donations. This suggests that collectivist culture encourages companies to be more socially responsible. The study also finds that CSR reduces firm risk more effectively in collectivist regions, as these cultures strengthen stakeholder relationships and reduce reputational risks. The findings are supported by international data, showing that both collectivism and individualism can positively influence CSR. Title: A meta-analysis of the impact of social media content strategies: the moderating role of culture
Authors: Fangfang Li, Leonidas C. Leonidou, Jieke Chen, Constantine S. Katsikeas
Abstract: Abstract Social media has become a strategic tool for firms worldwide to drive customer engagement (CE) and enhance business performance, yet limited research has systematically examined how social media content strategies (SMCSs) perform across cultural contexts. To address this gap, we conceptualize SMCS along three key dimensions—content characteristics, content source, and content valence—and develop a meta-analytic model grounded in signaling theory. Drawing on 148 empirical studies comprising 869 effect sizes, we examine the mediating role of CE, through which these content dimensions indirectly impact brand, product-market, and financial market performance. We also assess how national cultural values (i.e., individualism, uncertainty avoidance, power distance, masculinity, long-term orientation, and indulgence) moderate the content–engagement link. The findings reveal that CE serves as a key mechanism linking SMCSs to firm performance. Moreover, the strength and direction of these effects vary systematically across cultural values, highlighting important boundary conditions caused by national culture for social media content effectiveness. This study advances research at the intersection of social media and international business by providing a systematic cross-cultural account of how digital content strategies translate into engagement and performance outcomes.

Title: The two Coases of green governance: multinational enterprises and the internalization of environmental externalities through green innovation
Authors: Elizabeth Yi Wang, Jeremy Clegg, Jiahui Cheng
Abstract: Abstract Green governance aims to resolve environmental externalities at minimum cost. By uniting Coase's two foundational theories (Economica 4: 386–405, 1937; J Law Econ 3: 1–44, 1960) we reframe MNEs not merely as profit-seeking entities but as transnational institutions capable of internalizing environmental externalities through green innovation across borders. We show how national environmental regulation spurs subsidiary-level green patenting with profit spillovers into third-country markets, thereby yielding environmental benefits. Using data on over 1.4 million MNE-owned green patents (including 10,444 patents from 103 foreign subsidiaries of 89 MNEs, 1998–2014), we examine how host-country environmental regulatory stringency shapes subsidiary innovation. We find that a higher national mix of market-based over non-market regulatory stringency significantly increases local subsidiaries’ green patenting, and that green patenting in one jurisdiction enhances parent MNEs’ net profits in third-country markets. These effects suggest MNEs can operate as low-cost institutional engines of the Green Agenda by diffusing green innovation, complementing fragmented international governance efforts. They also imply that large economies can exercise policy leadership by prioritizing market-based regulation design that induces green innovation with cross-border benefits. Our Coasean approach to global environmental governance highlights MNEs’ promise for addressing grand challenges, particularly in extending the reach of the Green Agenda and in realizing the Sustainable Development Goals.

Title: Post-springboard growth of EMNEs: an asset orchestration perspective
Authors: Rishiraj Kashyap, Andreas Schotter, Prakash Satyavageeswaran, Snehal Awate
Abstract: Emerging-market multinational enterprises (EMNEs) are known for their asset-seeking strategies in foreign markets, often referred to as springboard strategies. While acquired assets strengthen EMNEs’ competitive position at home, it is not yet clear whether they lead to international growth when orchestrated across the enterprise. To address this gap, we apply an asset orchestration lens to EMNEs’ post-springboard international growth. Building on the EMNE-specific literature on light-touch integration, we study the role of headquarters–subsidiary linkages in enabling what we label as ‘autonomy-preserving asset orchestration’. We theorize that although such orchestration may improve international growth, its effectiveness reduces as the complexity of EMNEs’ asset portfolio increases. We attribute this reduction to the difficulty of multilateral coordination between subsidiaries through autonomy-preserving, light-touch mechanisms and without hierarchical structures. Using a novel dataset of foreign subsidiaries of Indian pharmaceutical multinationals, we find support for our arguments. Our study extends the springboard perspective by illuminating the post-springboard outcomes and contingencies associated with EMNEs’ autonomy-preserving asset orchestration. 新兴市场跨国企业（EMNEs）以其在海外市场中寻求资产的战略而闻名，这种战略通常被称为跳板战略。虽然所收购的资产增强了新兴市场跨国企业在本国市场的竞争地位，但当这些资产在整个企业范围内进行协调后是否能够带来国际增长，目前尚不明确。为了解决这一空白，我们运用资产编排的视角来研究新兴市场跨国企业在跳板战略之后的国际增长。基于关于新兴市场跨国企业的轻触式整合的相关文献，我们研究了总部与子公司之间的关联在促成我们称之为“保持自主性的资产编排”中所发挥的作用。我们提出理论：虽然这种编排方式可能促进国际增长，但随着新兴市场跨国企业资产组合复杂性的增加，其有效性会降低。我们将这种有效性的降低归因于通过保持自主性、轻触式机制且无层级结构进行子公司间多边协调的困难。利用关于印度制药跨国企业的海外子公司的新数据集，我们发现了支持我们论点的依据。我们的研究通过阐明与新兴市场跨国企业保持自主性的资产编排相关的后跳板后果及权变因素，扩展了跳板视角。 The article explores how emerging-market multinational enterprises (EMNEs), particularly in the Indian pharmaceutical industry, grow internationally by acquiring and managing foreign assets. It focuses on a strategy called "springboarding," where EMNEs acquire valuable assets abroad to strengthen their capabilities and expand their market presence. The study investigates how these companies manage acquired assets while maintaining the autonomy of the acquired firms, a method known as "autonomy-preserving asset orchestration." The key question is whether this approach leads to international growth and what limitations it might have. This article examines the international growth of Indian pharmaceutical EMNEs using a unique dataset of their foreign subsidiaries. The study focuses on how these companies manage their acquired assets without fully integrating them into their existing structures, allowing the acquired firms to retain some operational independence. This method, called "light-touch integration," contrasts with the more common approach of fully absorbing acquired firms. The researchers collected data from annual reports and conducted interviews with top management to understand how these companies maintain autonomy while creating collaborative linkages between the headquarters and subsidiaries. They used statistical methods, such as panel regressions, to analyze the relationship between this asset management approach and international growth. The study finds that autonomy-preserving asset orchestration positively impacts the international growth of EMNEs. Title: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West
Forecasting under uncertainty: import penetration and analysts’ cultural advantage
Abstract: The article explores the impact of Chinese import penetration on the accuracy of financial analysts’ earnings forecasts for U.S. manufacturing firms. The study is motivated by the geopolitical tensions between the U.S. and China, particularly during the Trump administration, which imposed tariffs on Chinese imports. This situation has raised questions about how international competition affects the information environment of U.S. firms. The study specifically examines how analysts’ cultural ties, particularly those of Chinese origin, influence their ability to forecast earnings accurately in the face of increased competition from Chinese imports. This article investigates the effects of Chinese import penetration on the accuracy of analysts’ earnings forecasts. It uses data from 504,491 earnings forecasts made by individual analysts from 2001 to 2024. The study measures Chinese import penetration at the industry level and examines its impact on forecast accuracy. The researchers find that increased Chinese import penetration generally reduces the accuracy of analysts’ forecasts. However, analysts of Chinese origin show a higher accuracy in their forecasts for firms facing significant Chinese import competition. The study suggests that these analysts’ cultural background and familiarity with Chinese business practices provide them with an informational advantage. The research also considers the role of industry experience and the concentration of Chinese analysts within industries and brokerages, finding that these factors further enhance the accuracy of forecasts made by Chinese analysts. The results indicate that Chinese import penetration decreases the accuracy of analysts’ forecasts by 12.1% on average. However, Chinese-origin analysts mitigate this effect, providing forecasts that are 33% more accurate than those of non-Chinese analysts. This advantage is particularly pronounced when these analysts have significant industry experience or when they operate in environments with a high concentration of Chinese analysts. The study concludes that cultural ties and industry expertise play a crucial role in improving forecast accuracy in the context of international competition. The findings highlight the importance of cultural diversity in financial markets and suggest that culturally informed analysis can enhance the interpretation of foreign-origin economic shocks. Future research could explore how these dynamics apply to other industries and regions, further enriching our understanding of global financial information processing. Title: Populism, regime characteristics, and MNC location choice
Authors: Srividya Jandhyala, Vera Kunczer, Thomas Lindner
Abstract: Abstract Countries with populist governments are less attractive investment destinations for Multinational Corporations (MNCs), as foreign firms tend to be delegitimized and targeted as members of the outgroup. However, populist governments vary in the extent to which they delegitimize foreign firms as outsiders. Departing from the traditional right–left classification that masks key differences among political regimes, this paper investigates aspects central to populism and to how populist governments see foreign firms: business orientation and stance on immigration. Pro-business regimes perceive a greater role for private sector firms and are less likely to treat MNCs as members of the outgroup. However, regimes with a strong anti-immigration stance highlight threats to local identity and are more likely to treat MNCs as members of the outgroup. Using a dataset of over 23,000 foreign direct investments (FDI) across 61 host countries from 2008 to 2017, we find that the adverse effect of populism on FDI is diminished in pro-business regimes whereas it is amplified in regimes with strong anti-immigration stances. Furthermore, regime alignment between home and host countries reduces the negative impact of populist governments on FDI. Our research highlights the crucial role of regime characteristics in shaping FDI across populist governments.

Authors: Konan Chan, De-Rong Kong, Tse-Chun Lin
Abstract: 我们研究了在企业不当行为爆发后，如何影响外国股票价格。我们发现，美国股市的投资者不仅会惩罚存在不当行为的公司，还会惩罚来自同一国家的其它外国公司，尤其是那些来自信誉较高国家的公司。这种效应在面临更大信息摩擦的外国公司中更为显著，例如存在严重信息不对称、财务可信度较弱的公司，或是那些在较弱制度环境中运营的公司。我们的研究结果表明，投资者会在外国股票估值中计入“信任溢价”，但当一个国家的可信度因其关联公司的不当行为而受损时，投资者便会撤回这一溢价。 Reputation plays a crucial role in markets, influencing how participants engage in exchanges. When a firm's information is unclear, outsiders often rely on group-level cues, like a country's reputation, to make judgments. This study explores how the U.S. market reacts to changes in collective reputation, particularly when misconduct occurs. The research investigates whether a strong collective reputation buffers or amplifies the fallout from misconduct, especially in environments with varying levels of information transparency and institutional strength. This article examines U.S.-listed foreign firms from the same country, termed a country affinity group, to study the impact of collective reputations. By focusing on these groups, the study minimizes concerns about firms strategically sorting themselves into different groups. The research uses corporate misconduct disclosures from RavenPack News Analytics to identify reputational shocks and measures a country's collective reputation using LSEG MarketPsych Analytics, which analyzes news and social media for trustworthiness. The study finds that investors in the U.S. stock market assess foreign stocks not only by firm-level traits but also by their country of origin, using collective reputation as a quality signal. This can create a "trust premium" for firms from reputable countries. However, when misconduct occurs, this trust premium can quickly turn into a liability, leading to a decline in stock prices. The results show that stock returns of country affinity groups from more trustworthy countries decline more sharply after misconduct disclosures than those from less trustworthy countries. This supports the hypothesis that investors incorporate a trust premium into stock prices, highlighting the importance of collective reputations in price formation. The study also finds that firms with lower reporting credibility and greater information asymmetry experience larger stock price declines following misconduct news. Institutional strength plays a moderating role, with stronger institutions helping to insulate firms from reputational shocks. Overall, while collective reputations provide a trust premium that enhances firm value, they also increase exposure to risk when compromised. The study concludes that collective reputations significantly impact firm value, especially in environments with less credible firm-level information and weaker institutions. This has important implications for foreign firms considering listing on the U.S. stock market, as country trustworthiness is a critical factor in overseas listing decisions. Future research could explore how reputation effects influence financing conditions and cross-border mergers and acquisitions, providing deeper insights into the dynamics between collective reputations and firm-level financial outcomes. Title: Emerging government export support programs: synergistic interaction with traditional programs and export performance consequences
Authors: Khuram Shahzad, Di Fan, Carl F. Fey, Daekwan Kim, Wei Liu
Abstract: 尽管以往的出口文献中的研究已经探讨了政府如何利用出口支持计划 (ESP) 来加强中小企业 (SME) 的学习和联结机制以提升出口竞争力, 一种新兴的、专注于提升生产能力的ESP类型的作用仍然未被充分研究。基于组合逻辑 (compositional logic) 和“杠杆-联结-学习” (LLL) 国际化框架, 本研究将一种新兴的基于公共设施中心 (CFC) 的ESP概念化为杠杆导向型, 同时将传统计划归类为学习和联结导向型的ESP。鉴于ESPs在新兴市场中更为突出, 我们利用2019至2022年间150家巴基斯坦SME的匹配数据, 研究了基于CFC的ESP的直接影响及其与传统ESP相结合时对SME出口绩效的协同影响。本研究发现, 参与CFC不仅直接提升了企业的出口能力, 还增强了杠杆导向型和学习导向型计划的有效性, 尤其是在新兴市场的背景下。此外, 将基于CFC的ESP与传统ESP相结合的协同效应在SME的吸收能力较强时进一步得到强化, 这凸显了内部能力在最大化外部支持收益中的作用。通过率先将聚焦生产能力的CFC作为杠杆导向型ESP进行研究, 本论文扩展了SME国际化的文献, 并为新兴市场的政策制定者和管理者提供了实践性的洞见, 帮助他们将政府支持与企业层面能力相结合, 以实现更优越的出口成果。 Embora pesquisas anteriores na literatura sobre exportação tenham examinado como os governos utilizam programas de apoio à exportação (ESPs) para fortalecer os mecanismos de aprendizado e conexão de pequenas e médias empresas (SMEs) em prol da competitividade exportadora, o papel de um tipo emergente de ESP—focado no aprimoramento das capacidades produtivas—permanece pouco explorado. Com base na lógica composicional e no modelo de internacionalização Leverage–Linkage–Learning (LLL), este estudo conceitualiza um novo tipo emergente de ESP baseado em Centros de Facilidades Comuns (CFCs), que visa aprimorar as capacidades produtivas como um tipo orientado à alavancagem, enquanto classifica programas tradicionais como ESPs orientados ao aprendizado e à conexão. Dado que ESPs são mais relevantes em mercados emergentes, examinamos tanto os efeitos diretos de ESPs baseados em CFCs quanto o impacto sinérgico de ESPs combinados com ESPs tradicionais sobre o desempenho exportador de SMEs, utilizando um conjunto de dados emparelhados de 150 SMEs paquistanesas entre 2019 e 2022. Este estudo conclui que a participação em CFCs não apenas melhora diretamente as exportações das empresas, mas também amplifica a eficácia dos programas orientados à alavancagem e ao aprendizado, particularmente no contexto de mercados emergentes. Além disso, os efeitos sinérgicos da combinação de ESPs baseados em CFCs e ESPs tradicionais são ainda mais fortalecidos pela capacidade de absorção de SMEs, o que destaca o papel das capacidades internas na maximização de benefícios do apoio externo. These challenges include a lack of understanding of foreign markets and limited resources. This is especially true for manufacturing SMEs in emerging markets, which often struggle with outdated technology and negative perceptions of product quality. To help SMEs overcome these barriers, governments have introduced export support programs (ESPs) that provide resources like market intelligence, networking opportunities, and financial assistance. However, there is limited research on the effectiveness of these programs, particularly those that offer access to modern production facilities and technological consulting. This article explores the impact of a new type of ESP that focuses on providing SMEs with access to advanced production and R&D facilities, known as Common Facility Centers (CFCs). The study examines how these leverage-oriented ESPs, when combined with traditional linkage- and learning-oriented programs, affect SME export performance. The research uses data from Pakistani SMEs that participated in government ESPs, analyzing their export performance over several years. Title: Media as nonmarket influencer in international business
Authors: Yadong Luo, Anlan Zhang, Tony Fang
Abstract: Abstract Media has emerged as a powerful yet under-theorized force shaping the nonmarket environments of multinationals (MNEs), particularly amid intensifying geopolitical tensions and ideological polarization. Drawing on mass communication theory, we conceptualize media, encompassing both institutional news media and social media platforms, as a distinct nonmarket influencer that actively constructs legitimacy, propagates geopolitical narratives, and accelerates public sentiment across borders. We develop a framework that explicates the pathways through which media reconfigures nonmarket influences facing MNEs, including legitimacy arbitration, geopolitical narrative, sentiment cascades, and shaping liabilities of foreignness and origin across interconnected home, host, and global arenas. We advance media literacy as a form of corporate soft power that enables MNEs to sense media-driven threats, seize narrative opportunities, and reconfigure communication structures as part of an integrated nonmarket strategy and corporate diplomacy. By repositioning media as a constitutive force rather than a peripheral communication channel, we present a foundation for understanding how MNEs develop their capacity to anticipate media-driven risks, manage legitimacy across borders, and adapt nonmarket strategies under geopolitical and ideological uncertainty.

Title: R&D location choice under technology sanctions: evidence from Chinese MNEs
Authors: Chenjian Zhang, Zhenyuan Xu, Kejing Chen, Hanwen Sun
Abstract: The article explores how technology sanctions, particularly those imposed by the United States on Chinese firms, affect the location choices for research and development (R&D) subsidiaries of multinational enterprises (MNEs). These sanctions are part of a broader trend of techno-nationalism, where countries view control over technology as crucial for national security and economic competitiveness. The study investigates how these sanctions influence where MNEs establish new R&D subsidiaries, considering geopolitical tensions and the need for economic connectivity. This article uses a difference-in-differences design to analyze data from 141,440 firm-year-country observations between 2014 and 2023. The study focuses on Chinese MNEs affected by U.S. technology sanctions and examines how these firms reconfigure their R&D locations. The research considers factors such as international political relationships, host country governance quality, and domestic political connections. The study uses the U.S. Entity List designations as external shocks to test its hypotheses. The analysis reveals that technology sanctions change the traditional factors influencing R&D location choices. Strong governance quality, usually seen as an advantage, may become a liability under sanctions due to increased compliance risks. The study also identifies a "triangular offset" pattern, where MNEs prefer countries with weaker ties to the sanctioning power, and highlights the role of home-country political connections in enabling firms to adapt their R&D strategies. The results show that Chinese MNEs exposed to U.S. technology sanctions tend to establish new R&D subsidiaries in countries with weaker bilateral relations with the U.S. and lower governance quality. These countries offer geopolitical insulation and economic connectivity, making them attractive locations for R&D activities. The study concludes that technology sanctions reshape the conventional logic of R&D location choices, emphasizing the importance of geopolitical and geo-economic factors. The findings suggest that home-country political connections play a crucial role in enabling firms to navigate these challenges and establish new R&D subsidiaries. The study's insights have implications for understanding how MNEs adapt to geopolitical tensions and the role of technology in international competition. Future research could explore how MNEs from other countries respond to different sanction regimes and the impact on innovation quality. Title: High involvement–low investment foreign operating mode: considering Indian MNEs in emerging markets
Authors: Rishiraj Kashyap, Andreas Schotter, Prakash Satyavageeswaran, Elizabeth L. Rose
Abstract: This article explores how Indian multinational enterprises (MNEs) successfully operate in foreign markets using non-equity modes, such as partnerships, rather than direct investments. Traditionally, it is believed that MNEs should invest in local firms to access valuable local resources and minimize transaction costs. However, the study finds that Indian MNEs often thrive without such investments, especially in emerging markets where relationship networks are crucial. This challenges the conventional asset-bundling view, which suggests that non-equity modes are inefficient for combining intangible assets. This article uses a multiple case study approach to understand how Indian MNEs manage to sustain non-equity operations. The researchers conducted 51 interviews with executives from nine Indian MNEs operating in 62 emerging markets. They focused on how these companies bundle their consultative selling skills with local partners' relationship networks. The study reveals that MNEs engage deeply with their partners, demonstrating commitment through high managerial involvement. This involvement includes co-selling, marketing, capability building, and long-term planning. MNEs also screen partners for alignment in values and dependence on the MNE for revenue, which helps build trust and sustain partnerships. The findings show that high managerial involvement helps MNEs build trust with partners, allowing them to bundle intangible assets effectively. This approach enables MNEs to maintain successful operations without equity investments, even in challenging markets. The study contributes to the literature by highlighting the importance of managerial involvement as a form of market commitment, distinct from financial investment. It suggests that MNEs can achieve sustained growth through non-equity modes by leveraging relational assets and maintaining strong partner relationships. In conclusion, the study provides a new perspective on foreign market entry strategies, emphasizing the role of managerial involvement in sustaining non-equity operations. This approach allows MNEs to navigate the complexities of emerging markets without the risks associated with direct investments. Future research could explore how these strategies apply to other contexts and industries, potentially offering a model for MNEs seeking to expand internationally with minimal investment risk.
