Authors: Sjoerd Beugelsdijk, Michele J Gelfand, Johannes Kleinhempel

Title: Manufacturing national consent for industrial policy: a microhistorical analysis of Finnish shipbuilding
Abstract: Abstract Industrial policy, the use of state power to influence the development of industries, has become increasingly influential in international business, yet its firm-level dynamics remain understudied. Through a history-to-theory approach and microhistorical analysis, we investigate how the Finnish shipbuilding industry employed nonmarket strategies (NMS) to influence outward-oriented industrial policies that supported its international expansion. Grounded in New Institutional Economics, we identify two key industrial policy shifts – in the mid-1950s and early 1980s – that reduced cross-border transaction costs for Finnish shipbuilders to enhance their international competitiveness. Before each shift, the industry proactively aligned its business interests with national policy priorities, engaging in what we term “manufacturing national consent” – positioning the sector as critical to national interests to legitimize supportive policies. We critically assess the double-edged role of NMS in industrial policy, demonstrating that while it creates regulatory capture and hinders alternative economic pathways, it also fosters government–business collaboration, improving the prospects of effective policy design. We further account for country-specific factors and broader inter-country dynamics to analyze policy implications for home-country firms. In all, our study contributes to the revitalization of industrial policy as a topic in the IB discipline by uncovering the active role of firms in shaping policy outcomes.

Title: The spirit of the times: historical conditions and market-seeking FDI strategies by U.S. alcohol firms
Authors: Xuchang Chen, Vladislav Maksimov, Blake Dustin Mathias, Stephanie Lu Wang
Abstract: Abstract Market-seeking foreign direct investment (FDI) remains central for firms to expand their global presence and seize opportunities abroad. However, existing research often focuses on immediate or near-term drivers related to firms’ market-seeking FDI strategies, and thus neglects the valuable insights a historical perspective can provide. To address this gap, we draw insights from imprinting theory and propose a framework theorizing the dual-layered imprinting of historical conditions stemming from both extreme historical experiences and founding conditions. Using the U.S. alcohol industry as a research context, we employ a mixed-methods approach, integrating quantitative and qualitative techniques. Our findings reveal that firms’ experiences during extreme anti-alcohol conditions, such as Prohibition, positively correlate with regulation-driven market-seeking FDI, while firms founded in more pro-alcohol periods prioritize speed-driven market-seeking FDI. Moreover, we identify how unrelated diversification, a strategy consistent with the anti-alcohol imprint but inconsistent with the pro-alcohol imprint, affects the relationship between historical imprints and FDI strategies through imprint amplification or decay. Our qualitative analyses elucidate the role of founders’ and leaders’ strategic decision-making in reinforcing the mechanisms through which historical conditions shape FDI strategy. This longitudinal framework provides insights into imprint formation, transmission, and manifestation, accounting for contextual variations and implications for FDI strategy.

Title: Artificial states, ethnicity, and the survival of private participation infrastructure projects in Africa
Abstract: Abstract Despite increasing interest, research within the context of Africa, particularly in relation to its unique historical dynamics, remains relatively underexplored in international business (IB). ​Our paper explores how colonial-era historical legacies continue to shape the outcomes of present-day private participation infrastructure (PPI) projects in Africa. By analyzing 301 PPI projects across 102 ethnic groups in 32 African countries, we offer insights into how borders misaligned with pre-colonial ethnic boundaries contribute to conflicts that undermine project viability. The findings reveal that ethnic partitioning, defined as the division of ethnic groups across artificial national borders, negatively impacts PPI project survival, with conflict mediating this relationship. While higher institutional quality mitigates these adverse effects, its impact remains marginal. We incorporate historical perspectives and highlight the importance of considering the path dependence of contemporary institutional environments. It also addresses the growing demand for Africa-focused IB research. By incorporating ethnicity into institutional analyses, our study also challenges the traditional IB assumption regarding the primacy of national borders in business activities. Our study points to the importance of understanding historical backgrounds when doing business in Africa.

Title: When does historical context matter? Explaining the emergence of competence-creating subsidiaries
Authors: Andrew C. Godley, Shane Hamilton, Marrisa Joseph
Abstract: Abstract Despite thorough attention to how context shapes subsidiary behavior, very little IB research has explored the dynamic impact of disruptive changes in historical context on organizational innovations in MNEs. Existing IB theory has robustly theorized the growth of competence-creating subsidiaries from the 1980s to the 2000s. However, our historical research demonstrates that this body of existing theory fails to explain an equally significant growth in subsidiaries with protean competence-creating characteristics from 1945 to 1970. We show that the introduction of the U.K. National Health Service in 1948 precipitated a major upgrade of research capabilities among a near majority of the population of subsidiaries in U.K. pharmaceuticals by 1970. Synthesizing from both IB and literature on historical methods, we analyze the impact of this disruptive transformation in context, identifying the specific mechanisms that produced the rapid growth in what we identify as proto-competence-creating subsidiaries. This occurred in response to a dramatically new context, in ways that differ from those predicted by current theoretical explanations, and led to an institutional innovation hitherto unknown to IB. The implications of this are significant in a contemporary moment of rapid institutional disruption, when existing conceptualizations of subsidiary behavior may increasingly fail to capture real-world dynamics.

Title: Success and failure in family firm internationalization: The case of Rothschild
Authors: Liena Kano, Luciano Ciravegna, Andrew Johnston, Alain Verbeke
Abstract: Abstract In this study, we examine over 100 years of Rothschild’s international activity: we analyze this multinational enterprise’s (MNE’s) cross-border transfer of family-derived firm-specific advantages (FSAs) and the challenges of recombination thereof with novel resources. Family-derived FSAs hinge on the resources and features of the owning and controlling family. During the period of Rothschild’s international success in 19th-century Europe, the family itself served as a recombination mechanism for linking family-derived FSAs with complementary resources across borders. However, deploying family-derived FSAs in the American market and recombining these with nonfamily resources was hindered by bifurcation bias (a dysfunctional, affect-based heuristic characterizing family firms). We trace the manifestations of bifurcation bias over time and investigate its multifaceted impact on Rothschild’s internationalization. We suggest that effective resource recombination in host markets can be constrained by a two-stage authentication process. Here, the bifurcation bias in a first stage can influence which complementary resources in foreign markets will be accessed and how these will be integrated inside the firm. In a second stage, bifurcation bias can affect the functioning of the very actors supposed to be linking the complementary resources to be utilized and the extant, family-derived FSAs.

Title: Correction: Navigating geopolitical risks: How U.S. firms adjust supply chains amid U.S.–China rivalry
Authors: Bo Yang, Jinyuan Song, Yifan Wei, Jing Li

Title: Institutional investors, tax havens, and multinational subsidiaries
Authors: Nicole Choi, Han Donker, Mark Fedenia, John R. Nofsinger
Abstract: This article explores whether incorporating a firm in a tax haven is beneficial by examining the preferences of institutional investors. Tax havens offer lower tax rates, which can increase a firm's cash flow and value. However, they may also have weaker governance standards, potentially increasing agency costs and reducing firm value. The study investigates if institutional investors, who are typically well-informed, prefer firms incorporated in tax havens and how they balance the benefits of lower taxes against the risks of weaker governance. This article uses data from 15,537 institutional investors across 90 countries, covering 20,205 multinational companies (MNCs) from 2000 to 2021. It examines institutional ownership patterns to determine if investors favor firms in tax havens. The study considers various factors, including effective tax rates, governance indicators, and the presence of subsidiaries in tax havens. Effective tax rate difference is the difference between the tax rate in the firm's domicile country and the tax haven. The study categorizes institutional investors into independent (those without business ties to firms) and pressure-sensitive (those with business ties). The analysis uses panel regressions to assess the impact of tax rates and governance on institutional ownership. The results show that institutional ownership is higher for firms benefiting from lower taxes in tax havens, especially among independent institutions. These investors value both tax benefits and good governance. Pressure-sensitive institutions are less influenced by tax advantages and governance quality. The study also finds that institutional ownership is higher for firms with subsidiaries in tax havens, but the highest ownership occurs when firms are incorporated in tax havens. This suggests that incorporation in a tax haven is more attractive to institutional investors than merely having a subsidiary there. In conclusion, institutional investors tend to value the tax benefits of firms incorporating in tax havens, despite potential governance risks. The study highlights the importance of balancing tax advantages with governance standards. Future research could explore changes in ownership structure when firms change their country of incorporation or when tax haven countries adjust their governance policies. Policymakers might consider harmonizing tax and governance standards internationally to reduce the incentive for firms to incorporate in tax havens solely for tax benefits, while also protecting investors from governance risks. Este estudio investiga cómo los inversores institucionales se aproximan a las empresas multinacionales con vínculos con paraísos fiscales, analizando sus patrones de propiedad accionaria. Empleando datos trimestrales de tenencias de más de 15.000 inversionistas en 90 países y más de 20.000 empresas multinacionales, descubrimos que la propiedad institucional es notablemente mayor en las empresas constituidas en paraísos fiscales en comparación con aquellas que solo mantienen filiales allí. Los inversores muestran especial preferencia por la diferencia en las tasas impositivas entre el país de constitución de una empresa y su país de domicilio. Sin embargo, nuestros hallazgos revelan que los inversores institucionales no pasan por alto la importancia de un marco de gobernanza sólido. La propiedad institucional es mayor en empresas domiciliadas en países con estándares de gobernanza más fuertes, lo que sugiere un equilibrio entre los beneficios fiscales y los riesgos de gobernanza. Además, diferenciamos entre inversionistas institucionales independientes y aquellos dependientes (o sensibles a presión), encontrando que las instituciones independientes se centran particularmente en maximizar la eficiencia fiscal y garantizar una alta calidad de gobernanza, mientras que los inversionistas dependien

Title: Ethics in the editorial office: practical implications for managing journals
Abstract: For the Academy of International Business (AIB) journals, the Managing Editor’s role is to coordinate the peer-review and publication processes, serving as the central point of contact among the authors, reviewers, editorial team, and publisher. This position has been centrally located with the AIB Secretariat since 2007, allowing for continuity in managing JIBS’ review and publication process even as the person in the Editor-in-Chief (EIC) role changes at the end of an editorial term.

Title: The Helsinki internationalization process model: foundations and future agenda
Climate vulnerability and stock price crash risk worldwide
Authors: Xiaoran Ni, Yi Si, Bohui Zhang
Abstract: Usando um conjunto de dados global, documentamos que um aumento na vulnerabilidade climática em nível nacional, medido pela exposição, sensibilidade e capacidade adaptativa aos efeitos negativos de mudanças climáticas, resulta em um aumento no risco de queda abrupta no preço de ações no nível da firma. Entre esses componentes, a capacidade adaptativa apresenta poder explicativo mais proeminente e persistente. Confirmamos nossas principais descobertas utilizando uma abordagem com variável instrumental e explorando dois choques regulatórios que tendem a gerar variações globais ou intrapaíses na capacidade adaptativa. Além disso, mostramos que uma maior vulnerabilidade climática está associada a mais fracos fundamentos da empresa, maior retenção de más notícias agressivas e menor amplitude de propriedade institucional, todos fatores que tendem a desencadear futuras quedas nos preços de ações. Ademais, o efeito principal varia de acordo com diferenças institucionais ou culturais entre países. Nossas descobertas gerais indicam que a vulnerabilidade climática tem consequências adversas para o mercado de ações por meio de um pronunciado efeito desestabilizador. Essas descobertas destacam o papel crítico de instituições formais e informais na mitigação e adaptação a mudanças climáticas, uma questão importante para operações empresariais e formuladores de políticas em todo o mundo. Investidores internacionais e empresas multinacionais devem monitorar de perto políticas e iniciativas em nível nacional voltadas para o fortalecimento de resiliência climática ao selecionar investimentos e gerenciar cadeias de suprimentos globais. Nous appuyant sur un ensemble de données mondiales, nous démontrons qu'une augmentation de la vulnérabilité climatique au niveau du pays, mesurée par l'exposition, la sensibilité et la capacité d'adaptation aux effets négatifs du changement climatique, entraîne une augmentation du risque de krach boursier au niveau de l’entreprise. Parmi ces composantes, la capacité d'adaptation présente le pouvoir explicatif le plus important et persistant. Nous confirmons nos résultats principaux en utilisant une approche basée sur des variables instrumentales, et en explorant deux chocs réglementaires qui tendent à générer des variations intra-pays ou mondiales de la capacité d'adaptation. De plus, nous montrons qu'une plus grande vulnérabilité climatique est associée à des fondamentaux d'entreprise plus faibles, à une accumulation plus agressive de mauvaises nouvelles et à une base d'actionnaires institutionnels plus restreinte, autant de facteurs qui tendent à déclencher des krachs boursiers futurs. En outre, l'impact principal varie en fonction des différences institutionnelles ou culturelles entre les pays. Nos résultats globaux indiquent que la vulnérabilité climatique a des conséquences négatives sur le marché boursier en raison d'un effet déstabilisateur prononcé. Ces résultats mettent en lumière le rôle essentiel des institutions formelles et informelles dans l'atténuation du et l'adaptation au changement climatique - une question importante pour les opérations commerciales et les décideurs politiques du monde entier. Les investisseurs internationaux et les entreprises multinationales devraient surveiller de près les politiques et les initiatives au niveau du pays visant à renforcer la résilience climatique lorsqu'ils gèrent leurs chaînes d'approvisionnement mondiales et choisissent les organismes dans lesquels ils investissent. 利用全球数据集, 我们记录了国家层面气候脆弱性的增加 (通过对气候变化负面影响的暴露程度、敏感性和适应能力来衡量) 导致企业层面股价崩盘风险的增加。在这些组件中, 适应能力表现出了最突出和持久的解释力。我们使用工具变量法以及探索两种往往会导致全球或国内适应能力变化的监管冲击, 验证了我们的主要发现。此外, 我们表明, 更大的气候脆弱性与较弱的企业基本面、更激进的坏消息囤积以及更狭窄的机构持股范围相关, 而所有这些都可能引发未来的股价崩盘。此外, 这一主要效应因各国的制度或文化差异而异。我们的总体研究结果表明, 气候脆弱性通过显著的不稳定效应对股市产生不利影响。这些发现凸显了正式和非正式制度在减缓和适应气候变化方面的关键作用, 这对全球范围内的商业运营和政策制定者来说是一个重要问题。国际投资者和跨国公司在选择投资对象和管理全球供应链时, 应密切关注国家层面旨在增强气候韧性的政策和举措。 Using a global dataset, we document that an increase in country-level climate vulnerability, measured

Title: The data-based power of big-tech multinational enterprises
Authors: Ke Rong, Ronaldo Parente, Ziliang Deng, Zhengyao Kang, Ram Mudambi, William Newburry
Abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing recognition of digital globalization in international business (IB) literature, there is a more pressing need for a comprehensive understanding of the unprecedented power generated by big-tech multinational enterprises (MNEs). This paper suggests that harnessing data ubiquity globally, instantaneously, and continuously represents a defining feature and a revolutionary power source for big-tech MNEs. By leveraging global data value chains through a mutually reinforcing data-AI feedback loop of data access, analysis, and application, big-tech MNEs can reshape IB practices and challenge global regulatory frameworks. Drawing on power-dependence theory, our research framework highlights a logic of power mutuality characterized by the interplay between power generation and power counterbalance. These two forces provide a holistic lens for examining how big-tech MNEs create data-based power, but are simultaneously countered by the economic and sociopolitical stakeholders of big-tech MNEs. We propose promising avenues for future research on MNEs’ data strategies, global data value chains, foreignness and liabilities of data, and global data governance.

Title: Global investors, hidden suppliers: how institutions shape the impact of stock market liberalization programs on corporate responsibility
Authors: Shipeng Yan, Wei Jiang, Yue Xu
Abstract: 研究表明, 参与股票市场自由化计划的公司会接触到能够对管理决策施加跨境影响的全球投资者。因此, 随着全球投资者越来越多地采用环境、社会和治理 (ESG) 原则, 参与这些计划中的公司可能会增强其企业责任感和应对重大挑战的承诺。然而, 我们对这一文献提出质疑, 解释了为什么股票市场自由化计划的这种影响不应被视为理所当然, 尤其是在新兴市场, 并通过展示制度因素如何调节这一关系为该领域做出了贡献。利用中国的股票市场自由化计划作为将新兴市场公司与全球投资者准外生地联系起来的自然实验, 我们发现, 股票市场自由化计划中的新兴市场公司减少了供应商身份信息的披露, 这是应对重大环境挑战的重要一步。然而, 当新兴市场公司具有某些特征时, 例如大量的外资持股比例、全球环境认证以及具有海外经验的高层领导, 随着供应商自愿披露的长期好处和短期坏处之间的平衡发生变化, 这种负面影响就会减弱甚至逆转. The article explores the issue of supplier invisibility in global supply chains, which is a significant barrier to addressing environmental challenges. Many companies outsource their emissions to suppliers, making these suppliers the primary source of environmental harm. This is particularly problematic in emerging markets where regulatory oversight is weak. The study investigates whether firms in these markets disclose their suppliers’ identities more when they participate in stock market liberalization programs, which open them to global investors. The extant literature provides mixed predictions; while some suggest that firms increase transparency due to investor pressure, others argue firms reduce disclosure to avoid scrutiny. This article uses the Shanghai–Hong Kong and Shenzhen–Hong Kong Stock Connect programs as a research context. These programs allowed global investors to trade stocks in Chinese markets, increasing the influence of these investors on participating firms. The study employs a staggered difference-in-differences approach to assess the impact of these programs on supplier identity disclosure. The research also considers various factors that might influence disclosure, such as ownership by foreign investors, environmental certifications, and the overseas experience of company leaders. These factors are important because they can shift a firm’s focus from short-term risks to long-term benefits of transparency. The results indicate that firms tend to reduce supplier identity disclosure after participating in stock market liberalization programs. However, this trend is less pronounced in firms with significant foreign ownership, environmental certifications, or leaders with overseas experience. These characteristics help firms see the long-term benefits of transparency, such as improved reputation and investor relations. The study concludes that while global investors can drive positive change, supportive institutional environments are crucial for this to happen. Future implications suggest that policymakers should encourage long-term engagement with global investors and support firms in obtaining environmental certifications to enhance corporate responsibility. Research suggests that firms participating in stock market liberalization programs are exposed to global investors who can exert cross-border influence on management decisions. Accordingly, as global investors increasingly adopt environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles, firms in these programs may enhance their corporate responsibility and their commitment to addressing grand challenges. We challenge this literature by explaining why this effect of stock market liberalization programs should not be taken for granted, especially in emerging markets and contribute to the field by showing that institutional factors moderate this relationship. Using China’s stock market liberalization programs as natural experiments that quasi-exogenously connect emerging-market firms to global investors, we find that emerging-market firms in stock liberalization programs reduce their disclosure of supplier identity information, an important step in tackling environmental grand challenges. Title: Gender wage discrimination and the attractiveness of foreign MNC subsidiaries as employers for women
Authors: Wolfgang Sofka, Christoph Grimpe, Ulrich Kaiser
Abstract: Abstract Gender wage discrimination is a grand challenge that constrains economic growth worldwide and denies women fair opportunities. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how women’s own experiences of wage discrimination steer their career decisions. We adopt the perspective of job-seeking women and argue that prior exposure to wage discrimination reshapes their employer preferences. Specifically, it can flip the liability of foreignness typically faced by foreign MNCs into a perceived employer advantage because foreign MNCs can deviate from the host country’s gender-biased norms. We study this mechanism for 165,624 female professionals and managers who changed jobs in Denmark between 2002 and 2015, using a pay transparency law from 2006 for identifying the underlying mechanism. We find that women who have suffered larger wage discrimination in domestic employment are more likely to start working for foreign MNC subsidiaries. This effect is weaker in labor markets in which high-performing domestic employers can offer other benefits, such as reputation or job security. The effect is stronger when foreign MNC subsidiaries signal gender fairness through a higher share of women in management. Overall, our findings show how wage discrimination redirects female career paths, transforming a grand challenge into a strategic advantage for foreign MNCs.

Title: The global sourcing of green products
Authors: Heather Berry, Jasmina Chauvin, Yuxi Lance Cheng, Narae Lee
Abstract: Abstract Recent years have seen a rise in global trade of “green products”—those designed to minimize environmental harm compared to traditional alternatives. In this study, we examine the relevance of pollution haven effects—i.e., shifts of production toward countries with less stringent environmental standards—in firms’ global sourcing strategies for green products. Given the importance of credible and sustainable manufacturing practices in firms’ global value chains for green products, we expect that country environmental standards shape global sourcing decisions for green versus non-green products differently. Our findings using data on global imports and exports for more than 5000 distinct products over the 2002–2019 period show that green products are more likely to be sourced from countries with higher environmental stringency, whereas non-green product sourcing patterns align with prior research, which emphasizes the appeal of lower environmental standards and cost-efficiency. This green sourcing effect is stronger for consumer-facing products and for sourcing into countries where consumer engagement in environmentalism is higher and non-governmental organizations are more active. Unlike prior research that implies that higher environmental standards hurt exporters, our results suggest that such standards can benefit green product exporters.

Title: Global ecological dependence and multinationals’ climate innovation: the role of climate risk exposure and institutional conditions
Abstract: Abstract Climate change poses significant global challenges to multinational enterprises (MNEs). One crucial solution hinges on the development of new technologies to mitigate climate change or adapt to its adverse effects. However, it remains unclear what factors can effectively motivate MNEs’ development of climate innovation. Integrating the resource dependence theory and the natural resource-based view, we argue that MNEs’ strategies are shaped by their dependence on the global ecological environment for natural resources—coined here as global ecological dependence . When exposed to elevated climate risks, MNEs tend to engage in climate innovation to assuage the uncertainty associated with their global ecological dependence. This tendency is moderated by climate-related formal and informal institutions that alter the perceived benefits and costs of climate innovation: stringent regulatory demand for climate action weakens this tendency as it increases firm costs and can divert resources, whereas heightened societal demand enhances this tendency as it can increase MNEs’ perception of the benefits of climate innovation. We find evidence for our hypotheses in a panel of MNEs listed in the United States from 1995 to 2017. Our study contributes to resource dependence theory and extends our understanding of climate innovation as a viable solution to climate change.

Title: Principles of sustainable business: frameworks for corporate action on the SDGs
Third-country MNEs, trade wars, and competitive opportunities: a real-options perspective
Abstract: Abstract While geopolitical conflicts, including trade wars, have garnered substantial scholarly attention in recent years, the impact on the outsider firms not directly involved in such conflicts remains underexplored. Engaging in real-options informed analysis, we examine how MNEs from third countries may respond to trade wars by capitalizing on the potential for competitive opportunities: where trade wars prompt the scaling up of third-country subsidiary operations in the involved countries. We further explore how the strategic responses of third-country MNEs to the opportunities presented by a trade war can be enhanced by the strategic flexibility manifest in parent-MNE multinationality, the resources and networks embedded in local partners, and the presence of bilateral economic agreements. Employing the 2018 US–China trade war as an empirical context, our panel data encompass 3601 Chinese subsidiary operations for outsider MNEs hailing from 51 countries, which yields 14,404 annual subsidiary-level observations to conduct difference-in-differences analysis. The empirical results indicate that third-country MNEs disproportionately expanded their Chinese operations in response to the US–China tariff conflict, and that these strategic responses were pronounced for subsidiaries with highly multinational parents, local partnerships in the involved country, and a home–host country bilateral agreement.

Title: Home-country egalitarianism and cross-border nonmarket strategy
Authors: Jin Hyung Kim, Jordan I. Siegel
Abstract: La stratégie non-marchande transfrontalière – définie comme le choix par les entreprises multinationales en matière d'actions stratégiques non-marchandes dans le but de maximiser leur rentabilité sur un marché hôte - constitue une partie essentielle des affaires internationales. Des appels récents à la recherche affirment néanmoins que l'on sait encore très peu de choses sur la manière dont les entreprises multinationales choisissent parmi les stratégies non-marchandes transfrontalières. Nous proposons donc que l'égalitarisme - un type d'institution informelle propre au pays d'origine - est un facteur clé permettant de prédire un ensemble important de choix stratégiques non-marchands transfrontaliers, en particulier parmi les activités politiques des entreprises avec divers degrés de transparence. Nous testons également cet argument en intégrant une mesure de gouvernance d'entreprise au niveau de la firme, liée à la transparence, afin d'examiner comment cette gouvernance modère l'impact principal. Notre travail contribue à la recherche en stratégies non-marchandes et affaires internationales en mettant en lumière l'importance des institutions informelles du pays d'origine ainsi que des institutions formelles du pays d’accueil comme principes directeurs dans la stratégie non-marchande transfrontalière. 跨境非市场战略——跨国企业在东道国市场中为追求盈利而选择的非市场战略行动——是国际商业的重要组成部分。然而，近期的研究呼吁指出，人们对跨国企业如何选择跨境非市场战略知之甚少。因此，我们提出，平等主义（母国的非正式制度的一种）是一系列重要的跨境非市场战略选择的关键预测因素，特别是在具有不同透明度的企业政治活动中。我们通过纳入与透明度相关的企业层面的公司治理措施来进一步检验这一论点，以观察企业层面的公司治理如何调节主要效应。我们的研究通过强调母国非正式制度以及东道国正式制度在跨境非市场战略中的指导原则的重要性， 为国际商业和非市场战略研究做出了贡献。 La estrategia no-mercado transfronteriza, la elección de acciones estratégicas de no-mercado por parte de empresas multinacionales en busca de rentabilidad en un mercado anfitrión, es una parte esencial de losnegocios internacionales. Sin embargo, llamados recientes a la investigación afirman que se sabe muy poco sobre cómo las empresas multinacionales eligen entre estrategias de no-mercado transfronterizas. Por lo tanto, proponemos que el igualitarismo, un tipo de institución informal del país de origen, es un predictor clave de un conjunto importante de elecciones de estrategias no mercantiles transfronterizas, particularmente entre actividades políticas corporativas con diversos grados de transparencia. Además, ponemos a prueba este argumento incorporando una medida del gobierno corporativo a nivel empresarial relacionada con la transparencia para observar cómo la gobernanza corporativa a nivel empresarial modera el efecto principal. Nuestro estudio contribuye a la investigación sobre negocios internacionales y estrategias no-mercado al destacar la importancia de las instituciones informales del país de origen, así como de las instituciones formales del país anfitrión, como principio orientador en la estrategia no-mercado transfronteriza. A estratégia não-mercadológica transfronteiriça — a escolha de ações estratégicas não-mercadológicas por empresas multinacionais em busca de lucratividade em um mercado anfitrião — é uma parte essencial dos negócios internacionais. No entanto, solicitações recentes por pesquisas afirmam que se sabe muito pouco sobre como empresas multinacionais escolhem entre estratégias não-mercadológicas transfronteiriças. Assim, propomos que igualitarismo — um tipo de instituição informal do país de origem — é um preditor crucial de um conjunto importante de escolhas de estratégias não-mercadológicas transfronteiriças, particularmente entre atividades políticas corporativas com diferentes graus de transparência. Além disso, testamos esse argumento incorporando uma medida de governança corporativa em nível empresarial relacionada à transparência, para verificar como a governança corporativa em nível empresarial modera o efeito principal. Nosso estudo contribui para a pesquisa em negócios internacionais e estratégias não-mercadológicas ao destacar a importância de instituições informais do país de origem, bem como de instituições formai

Title: Innovate or litigate? The dual impacts of multimarket contacts on global competition
Authors: Claudio Giachetti, Ergun Onoz, Tieying Yu
Abstract: Abstract Our study, grounded in the multimarket competition, knowledge management, and technological change literature, investigates how multimarket contacts among multinational enterprises—i.e., the extent to which rival multinational enterprises meet simultaneously in multiple countries—shape their innovation and patent litigation decisions in host countries. We propose that the degree of multimarket contacts a multinational enterprise has with its competitors in a host country may restrain it from aggressively launching product and technological innovations in that country due to a fear of cross-country retaliation. However, increased multimarket contacts also facilitate knowledge diffusion, heightening the risk of imitation, and consequently enhance the multinational enterprise’s patent litigation intensity—a means to protect knowledge-based resources—in that country. Moreover, we examine how two features of the host-country technological environment—technological ferment (an era of intense technical variation following a technological discontinuity until a dominant design emerges) and home–host country differences in intellectual property protection—moderate these relationships. We test our hypotheses using a dataset of 85 mobile phone vendors, which includes data on their products and technological innovations and litigation cases in 46 countries between 2003 and 2015. This study sheds light on the interplay among multinational enterprises’ multimarket contacts, innovation, and patent litigation.

Title: Reframing social entrepreneurship in IB: from institutional constraints to generative processes in Creation Theory
Abstract: El artículo ganador del premio de la década de Stephan, Uhlaner y Stride (2015) destaca cómo los antecedentes institucionales formales e informales configuran el surgimiento del emprendimiento social en contextos transfronterizos, mientras que su retrospectiva de 2026 extendió la atención al impacto duradero de los emprendimientos sociales. El comentario de Reuber y Fischer (2026) amplió la conversación para enfatizar el impacto organizacional de los emprendimientos sociales. Sin embargo, aunque la retrospectiva y el comentario de Reuber y Fischer (2026) enfatizan cómo los emprendimientos sociales evolucionan y generan impacto a lo largo del tiempo, se quedan cortos en explorar plenamente cómo la acción emprendedora en sí misma da lugar a instituciones y grupos de interés. Este comentario se basa en el artículo ganador del premio, la retrospectiva y el comentario de Reuber y Fischer, mientras se fundamenta en la Teoría de la Creación (Alvarez & Barney, 2007; Alvarez & Sachs, 2023) para replantear el emprendimiento social como un proceso generativo en el que las oportunidades, las instituciones y los grupos de interés emergen conjuntamente a través de ciclos de acción, interpretación y experiencia compartida en condiciones de incertidumbre. Esta perspectiva muestra cómo los emprendedores y los grupos de interés no solo se adaptan a los entornos institucionales, sino que también los crean y reconfiguran activamente. Esta reformulación abre nuevas direcciones de investigación: examinar cómo los procesos emprendedores generan formas institucionales novedosas en contextos transfronterizos, cómo los roles de los grupos de interés se negocian y renegocian en diversos contextos culturales, y cómo los emprendimientos sociales transforman los propios contextos en los que operan. O artigo premiado com o Decade Award de Stephan, Uhlaner e Stride (2015) destaca como os antecedentes institucionais formais e informais moldam o surgimento do empreendedorismo social além-fronteiras, enquanto sua retrospectiva de 2026 amplificou a atenção para o impacto duradouro dos empreendimentos sociais. O comentário de Reuber e Fischer (2026) ampliou a conversa para enfatizar o impacto organizacional dos empreendimentos sociais. No entanto, embora a retrospectiva e o comentário de Reuber e Fischer (2026) enfatizem como empreendimentos sociais evoluem e geram impacto ao longo do tempo, eles não exploram completamente como a própria ação empreendedora traz à existência instituições e stakeholders. Este comentário baseia-se no artigo premiado, na retrospectiva e no comentário de Reuber e Fischer, ao mesmo tempo em que utiliza a Teoria da Criação (Alvarez & Barney, 2007; Alvarez & Sachs, 2023) para reformular o empreendedorismo social como um processo gerador em que oportunidades, instituições e stakeholders conjuntamente emergem por meio de ciclos de ação, interpretação e experiência compartilhada sob condições de incerteza. Essa perspectiva mostra como empreendedores e stakeholders não apenas se adaptam aos ambientes institucionais, bem como ativamente os criam e reconfiguram. Essa reformulação abre novas direções: examinar como processos empreendedores geram formas institucionais inovadoras além-fronteiras, como papéis de stakeholders são negociados e renegociados em diferentes contextos culturais e como os empreendimentos sociais transformam os próprios cenários nos quais operam. Title: Looking beyond institutional influences on social entrepreneurs: key issues and an agenda for future IB research on social venture impact
Abstract: Stephan, Uhlaner and Stride’s (2015) JIBS Decade Award-winning article provides a nuanced understanding of the national contexts that encourage social entrepreneurship. In this commentary, we build on their foundation and discuss the notion of social entrepreneurship further, shifting focus from individual engagement in social entrepreneurship to a consideration of social venture impact. This entails a shift from the individual as the unit of analysis to the social venture. Building on the ten years of social entrepreneurship research since Stephan, Uhlaner and Stride (2015) appeared, we examine the inevitable stakeholder multiplicity of social ventures, and the concomitant mission drift and mission motility that accompany it. We then discuss issues associated with measuring and scaling social venture impact, and options for studying the international factors affecting social venture impact. Throughout the article, we highlight the implications of these ideas for future international business research. More than a decade ago, researchers Ute Stephan, Lorraine Uhlaner, and Christopher Stride identified a gap in the systematic study of social entrepreneurship, entrepreneurship which addresses social needs, and noticed there was little comprehensive research on its global prevalence. They explored how formal and informal institutional factors influence individuals’ engagement in social entrepreneurship across 26 countries, involving over 100,000 participants. Their influential paper highlighted the importance of understanding the institutional context of social entrepreneurship and received the 2025 JIBS Decade Award. Their study found that supportive institutional environments, rather than institutional voids, are linked to higher engagement in social entrepreneurship. This article explores the concept of social venture impact, which refers to the effects a social venture has on its stakeholders, including unintended ones. It introduces key concepts like stakeholder multiplicity, mission drift, and mission motility. Stakeholder multiplicity involves managing diverse groups with varying interests, while mission drift refers to the shift towards commercial objectives at the expense of social goals. Mission motility involves deliberate changes in a venture’s mission. The article also discusses the challenges of measuring and scaling social venture impact, noting the difficulty in quantifying social performance compared to financial performance. It highlights the importance of finding scalable business models and the role of stakeholders in the scaling process. The article also examines how one might study the international impact of social venture comparatively to inform policymaking and practice. Title: Institutions and social entrepreneurship: a hierarchy of institutions to revisit institutional voids, support, and configurations
Authors: Ute Stephan, Lorraine M. Uhlaner, Christopher Stride
Abstract: Abstract In this retrospective, we expand on theorizing about institutions and social entrepreneurship (SE) as presented in our Decade Award-winning 2015 article. Our 2015 paper developed the institutional configuration perspective, which considers joint and interaction effects of formal and informal institutions. It organized disagreement about how formal institutions shape SE, contrasting the institutional voids and institutional support perspectives. In this retrospective, we introduce a revised hierarchy of institutions as a ‘middle-ground’ approach to advance research on institutions in international business and entrepreneurship. This hierarchy integrates insights from different disciplines (institutional economics, sociology, political science, and cultural theory). It explicates the macro-level economic and microfoundational psychological effects of four layers of formal (government activism and constitutional institutions/rule of law) and informal institutions (cultural values and norms). The hierarchy progresses research on institutional voids by distinguishing four types of formal and informal institutional voids. It advances research on institutional configurations by highlighting new synergistic and compensatory configurations. It also offers new insights into institutional change. Finally, we advance research on institutions and SE by theorizing a new institutional paradox for SE that reconciles the institutional void versus support debate and by charting opportunities for how institutions shape the SE process from entry to exit.

The nature and utility of cultural tightness–looseness: evidence for reconsideration
Authors: Michael Minkov, Plamen Akaliyski, Anneli Kaasa, Christian Welzel
Abstract: The concept of cultural tightness–looseness (TL) refers to how strictly societies enforce social norms and how much deviation from these norms is tolerated. This idea has been studied since the 1930s, but recent research has raised questions about its validity, especially when compared to individualism–collectivism (IC), which describes how societies prioritize individual versus group interests. This study reanalyzes data from Eriksson et al. to explore four main questions: how perceptions of societal norms relate to actual behaviors, what tight societies aim to regulate, how TL correlates with its supposed causes and effects, and whether attitudes to norm violations are influenced by TL. This article reexamines TL by analyzing data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and other sources. The researchers compared national scores based on societal impressions with self-reports of similar measures. They also looked at how TL relates to the acceptance of morally debatable behaviors and their supposed antecedents and consequences. The study used statistical methods like correlation and regression analysis to test these relationships. The researchers aimed to see if TL could be a distinct cultural dimension or if its effects are better explained by IC. They also examined whether TL influences societal reactions to norm violations, known as metanorms. The study found that TL does not significantly correlate with some self-reports of societal norms or behaviors. It also does not predict the acceptance of morally debatable behaviors after accounting for IC. The supposed causes and effects of TL, such as ecological threats or political freedom, were not significantly related to TL when IC was considered. The analysis showed that IC, not TL, better explains societal reactions to norm violations. These findings suggest that TL may not be a distinct cultural dimension and that many aspects attributed to TL might be better understood through IC. The study highlights the need to revise TL theory and better understand cultural norms, emphasizing the importance of IC in explaining societal behaviors. Future research should focus on refining the understanding of cultural dimensions and their implications. Title: The dual effects of geopolitical risk on MNCs’ first-tier supply base: a political economy perspective
Authors: Xuan Bai, Kevin Zheng Zhou, Bingkun Zhang, En Xie
Abstract: Mientras que investigaciones previas han enfatizado las amenazas económicas planteadas por el riesgo político, no está claro cómo el riesgo geopolítico (GPR, por sus siglas en inglés), un riesgo a nivel supranacional, afecta las decisiones relacionadas con las cadenas de suministro globales. Basándonos en la perspectiva de la economía política, postulamos que el riesgo geopolítico presenta tanto oportunidades como amenazas para las empresas multinacionales (MNCs, por sus siglas en inglés), dependiendo de la afinidad política entre los países de origen y anfitrión de las empresas multinacionales. También identificamos los roles de mitigación de riesgos que desempeñan el cabildeo político de las empresas multinacionales y la diversificación de mercados. Utilizando datos de panel de empresas multinacionales que cotizan en bolsa en los Estados Unidos, encontramos que el riesgo geopolítico del país anfitrión incrementa la base de suministro de primer nivel de las empresas multinacionales cuando la afinidad política entre el país de origen y el país anfitrión es alta, pero la reduce cuando la afinidad política es baja. Además, el efecto positivo del riesgo geopolítico del país anfitrión con alta afinidad sobre la base de suministro de las multinacionales es más fuerte, y el efecto negativo del riesgo geopolítico del país anfitrión con baja afinidad es más débil para las empresas multinacionales con altos niveles de cabildeo político o diversificación de mercados. Estos hallazgos enriquecen la investigación en negocios internacionales y la perspectiva de la economía política al elucidar tanto las oportunidades como las amenazas del riesgo geopolítico, y destacan la importancia de las capacidades para enfrentar riesgos en la gestión del riesgo geopolítico. Estos hallazgos también proporcionan perspectivas para que las empresas multinacionales adapten sus estrategias en medio del riesgo geopolítico, aprovechando la afinidad política entre los países de origen y anfitrión, participando en lobby político y buscando la diversificación de mercados para mitigar los desafíos geopolíticos. 尽管先前的研究强调了政治风险带来的经济威胁, 尚不清楚地缘政治风险 (GPR) 这种超国家层面的风险如何影响全球供应链决策。借鉴政治经济学的视角, 我们认为GPR对跨国公司 (MNCs) 既带来机遇, 又带来威胁, 这取决于MNC本国与东道国之间的政治亲和度。我们还确定了MNC的政治游说和市场多元化能力对风险的缓解作用。通过使用来自美国上市的MNC的面板数据, 我们发现, 当本国与东道国之间的政治亲和度较高时, 东道国的GPR会使MNC的一线供应基地增加; 而当政治亲和度较低时, 则会减少。此外, 当MNC有较高的政治游说和市场多元化能力时，高亲和度东道国的GPR对MNC供应基地的积极影响增强, 而低亲和度东道国的GPR的负面影响减弱。这些研究结果通过阐明GPR的机遇和威胁, 丰富了国际商务研究和政治经济学的视角, 并突出了风险应对能力在管理GPR中的重要性。这些发现还为MNC在GPR中调整战略提供了洞见, 即通过利用本国与东道国之间的政治亲和度、参与政治游说以及追求市场多元化来缓解地缘政治挑战。 While prior research has emphasized the economic threats posed by political risk, it is unclear how geopolitical risk (GPR), a supranational-level risk, affects global supply chain decisions. Drawing on the political economy perspective, we posit that GPR presents both opportunities and threats for multinational corporations (MNCs), depending on the political affinity between MNCs’ home and host countries. We also identify the risk-mitigation roles of MNCs’ political lobbying and market diversification. Using panel data from publicly listed MNCs in the US, we find that host-country GPR increases MNCs’ first-tier supply base when home–host country political affinity is high, but decreases when political affinity is low. Moreover, the positive effect of high-affinity host-country GPR on MNCs’ supply base is stronger, and the negative effect of low-affinity host-country GPR is weaker for MNCs with high levels of political lobbying or market diversification. These findings enrich the international business research and political economy perspective by elucidating both the opportunities and threats of GPR, and highlight the importance of risk-coping capabilities in managing GPR. These findings also provide insights for MNCs to adapt their strategies amid GPR by leveraging home–host political affinity, engaging in political lobbying, and pursuing market diversification to mitigate geopolitical challenges. Title: The insights from the crowd: Drawing inferences from many approaches to key empirical questions in international business
Authors: Andrew Delios, Tianyou Hu, Shu Yu, Nan Zhou, Faisal M. Ahsan, Mona Bahl, Tao Bai, Madhurima Basu, Hanoku Bathula, Georgios Batsakis, Jorge Carneiro, Dwarka Chakravarty, Danyang Chen, Weihong Chen, Ying-Yu Chen, Luis Alfonso Dau, Shu Deng, Desislava Dikova, Xiaomin Fan, Viswa Prasad Gada, Dongdong Huang, Hyun Gon Kim, Kyungjoong Kim, Aleš Kubíček, Chengguang Li, Wen Helena Li, Yi Li, Yuanyuan Li, Yung-Chih Lien, Huanchen Liu, Wei Liu, Grigorij Ljubownikow, Racheal Louis Vincent, Ondřej Machek, Parul Manocha, Yoichi Matsumoto, Atthaphon Mumi, Chao Niu, N. Nuruzzaman, Vidya Sukumara Panicker, K. Praveen Parboteeah, Wei Qiao, Xiaole Qiao, Shyamala Sethuram, Ao Shen, Lei Shi, Evis Sinani, Sandeep Sivakumar, Pei-Shan Soon, Maximilian Stallkamp, Priit Tinits, Daniel Tolstoy, Andranik Tumasjan, Mayank Varshney, Andres Velez-Calle, Chris Wagner, Peng Wang, Xingang Wang, Yong Wang, Liang Wen, Tao Wu, Sandeep Yadav, Jiaju Yan, Jing Yu Yang, Megan Zhang, Weihao Zhang, Yameng Zhang, Yang Zhao, Eric Uhlmann
Abstract: Abstract In this crowdsourced initiative, 57 independent analysts used the same longitudinal dataset to address four major empirical questions in international business. For all four research questions, different analysts obtained substantial estimates in opposite directions, meaning that they could have drawn any conclusion at all had they conducted the project alone. Aggregating across the results obtained by different analysts pointed to an overall answer for two of the four research questions, although for one of the two questions, the evidence was more suggestive than conclusive. That said, the variability in results was not simply random, and could in some cases be meaningfully explained. Choices regarding how to operationalize variables played an important role in determining the empirical results, and expert analysts were more likely to report large positive effects. Rather than exhibiting a bias to confirm their pre-existing beliefs, analysts appeared to rationally update their beliefs considering the evidence. Overall, these findings empirically demonstrate the role of subjective researcher choices in shaping results in international business research yet also show that it is still possible to draw meaningful conclusions in science. We advocate for an open science of international business in which the consequences of subjective analytic choices are rendered as transparent as possible.

Title: Long-run post-event returns in global stock markets
Authors: Hendrik Bessembinder, Michael J. Cooper, Wei Jiao, Feng Zhang
Abstract: Firms often experience significant abnormal stock returns following major corporate events, but these returns vary widely across countries. We examine how national institutions—particularly financial system development, investor protection, and governance practices—influence post-event stock returns for over 164,000 events across 58 countries. Our analysis covers six frequent corporate events: dividend initiations, share repurchases, seasoned equity offerings, stock splits, mergers and acquisitions, and initial public offerings. Using a characteristic-based benchmarking approach that accounts for cross-country differences in firm fundamentals, we find that firms in countries with more developed financial systems and stronger investor protections exhibit significantly smaller long-run post-event abnormal returns. These findings are robust to alternative benchmarks and model specifications. Our results suggest that the institutional environment can reduce informational frictions and promote more efficient investor responses to corporate announcements. In countries with strong financial and governance institutions, market reactions to corporate events are more muted—indicating fewer pricing anomalies and more efficient capital markets. By demonstrating how national institutions help shape the outcomes of firm-level events, our study highlights the value of incorporating institutional context into international finance research and helps explain why post-event return patterns often differ across countries. Corporate event studies have long helped us understand how investors react to major financial decisions by companies. While much research has focused on U.S. markets, less attention has been given to post-event returns in global markets. This study aims to fill that gap by examining how stock returns behave after corporate events in non-U.S. markets, using a broad global sample and consistent research methods. This article first reviews 75 studies on post-event stock returns outside the U.S., covering 100 country-event studies. It finds significant differences in conclusions among these prior studies, indicating a need for a more systematic approach. The study then analyzes 51,802 stocks from 58 countries, focusing on six corporate events: initial public offerings (IPOs), seasoned equity offerings (SEOs), stock repurchases, stock splits, dividend initiations, and mergers and acquisitions. The dataset spans from 1996 to 2020 and includes nearly 165,000 corporate events. The study compares the post-event returns of event firms to non-event firms, using three types of benchmarks: a zero benchmark, size and book-to-market matched firms, and a characteristic-based benchmark. The study finds that global post-event returns generally align with U.S. findings, when analyzing mean adjusted returns and returns adjusted by size and book-to-market-matched control firms. It also shows that these abnormal returns can largely be explained by firm characteristics when using a characteristic-based benchmark. This finding suggests that the apparent abnormal returns are not as unusual as previously thought. The study further documents that post-event returns are influenced by country-specific factors like market size, liquidity, and investor protection. Smaller, less developed, and more volatile markets show greater abnormal returns, while countries with better investor protections and market-oriented financial systems show smaller abnormal returns. In conclusion, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of post-event returns in global markets, highlighting the importance of firm characteristics and local market conditions. It suggests that future research should consider these factors to better understand investor reactions to corporate events. This has implications for investors, policymakers, and corporate managers, as it emphasizes the need for consistent methods and consideration of local market conditions in evaluating corporate events. Multihoming: an internationalization strategy in a world of artificial intelligence ecosystems
Authors: Shihao Zhou, Shaoqin Tang, Daitian Li, Tony W. Tong
Abstract: 随着人工智能 (AI) 日益渗透到国际商业 (IB) 中, 它为IB研究提出了两个关键问题: 1) AI如何重塑企业国际化的外部环境?以及2) 企业如何在AI转型的环境中调整其国际化战略?针对第一个问题, 我们认为AI时代的特征在于多个AI生态系统的共存——每个生态系统都植根于一个国家的AI行业体系, 而通过参与者跨生态系统的活动在全球范围内相互连系。 针对第二个问题, 我们提出了“多栖” (multihoming) 战略, 即企业同时在多个AI生态系统中运营, 作为在这一新环境下的国际化策略。 我们确定了这一“多栖”视角的三个独特特征, 并探讨了它如何在扩展现有的IB理论的同时深化我们对企业国际化的理解。 À medida que a inteligência artificial (AI) permeia cada vez mais os negócios internacionais (IB), ela levanta duas questões críticas para a pesquisa em IB: 1) Como a AI remodela o ambiente externo para a internacionalização de empresas? e 2) Como empresas adaptam suas estratégias de internacionalização nesse cenário transformado pela AI? Para abordar a primeira pergunta, argumentamos que a era da AI é caracterizada pela coexistência de múltiplos ecossistemas de AI — cada um enraizado no sistema setorial nacional de AI de seu respectivo país, porém interconectado globalmente por meio de atividades entre ecossistemas de seus participantes. Para abordar a segunda pergunta, propomos o multihoming — empresas que operam simultaneamente em múltiplos ecossistemas de AI — como uma estratégia de internacionalização nesse novo contexto. Identificamos três características distintivas dessa perspectiva de multihoming e discutimos como ela avança nossa compreensão sobre a internacionalização de empresas, ao mesmo tempo em que expande teorias existentes em IB. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming businesses worldwide. While much research has focused on how AI affects internal management, less is known about its impact on the external business environment. This article explores how AI reshapes the international business landscape and how firms adapt their strategies in this new context. The study introduces the concept of "country-rooted global AI ecosystems," which are networks of AI actors that are both locally grounded and globally connected. It also examines how firms can use a strategy called "multihoming" to operate across multiple AI ecosystems simultaneously. This article investigates the emergence of country-rooted global AI ecosystems, which are defined by their unique technological, market, and institutional characteristics. These ecosystems consist of various actors, including technology creators, suppliers, and regulators, who work together to create value. The study highlights the importance of understanding AI through an ecosystem lens, as these ecosystems are not easily transferable across borders due to their specific investments and architectures. The article also discusses the global aspect of AI ecosystems, emphasizing the open-source nature of AI technologies and the global distribution of strategic assets needed for AI development. The study concludes that AI firms can benefit from multihoming, which involves participating in multiple AI ecosystems to expand their consumer base and leverage data network effects. However, multihoming also presents challenges, such as the need to adapt to different ecosystem architectures and manage geopolitical tensions. The authors argue that multihoming offers a unique internationalization strategy that differs from traditional approaches, as it requires firms to navigate complex interdependencies within and across ecosystems. The study suggests that future research should explore how AI firms can strategically engage with multiple ecosystems to maintain flexibility and competitiveness in a rapidly evolving global landscape. Title: Inward foreign direct investment and technological innovation of local firms: differential impacts on incremental and radical innovation
Abstract: 外商直接投资 (FDI) 是促进还是抑制本地企业的技术创新?先前的研究对这一重要问题产生了不同的观点和结论。为了解决这一难题, 我们提出FDI溢出效应和挤出效应可能分别作用于创新的不同阶段 (即创意生成和研发实施) , 从而导致FDI对渐进式创新和突破式创新的不同影响。中国上市公司面板数据的研究结果表明, 行业层面的FDI与渐进式创新呈正相关, 而对突破式创新的影响呈倒U型关系。此外, 我们发现技术差距强化了FDI对渐进式创新的正向影响, 同时使其对突破式创新的倒U型影响更加显著, 并且当FDI的本地市场关注度越高时, FDI与突破式创新之间的倒U型关系越陡峭。这些发现调和了关于FDI如何影响本地创新的不一致性, 并为FDI文献提供了一个新颖的分析框架。 Does inward foreign direct investment (FDI) promote or inhibit the technological innovation of local firms? Prior research has generated mixed views and findings on this important question. To address this puzzle, we propose that FDI spillover and crowding-out effects may apply to different phases of innovation (i.e., idea generation and R&D implementation) respectively, which then leads to differential impacts of FDI on incremental and radical innovation. The results from a panel dataset of Chinese listed firms show that industry-level FDI is positively related to incremental innovation but has an inverted U-shaped impact on radical innovation. Furthermore, we find that technology gap reinforces the positive impact of FDI on incremental innovation while making its inverted U-shaped impact on radical innovation more pronounced, and when FDI local market focus is higher, the inverted U-shaped relationship between FDI and radical innovation is steeper. These findings reconcile the inconsistency regarding how FDI may affect local innovation and provide a novel analysis framework for the FDI literature. L’investissement direct étranger ( Foreign Direct Investment - FDI) entrant favorise-t-il ou inhibe-t-il l’innovation technologique des entreprises locales ? Les recherches antérieures ont apporté des points de vue et des résultats divergents sur cette question importante. Pour résoudre cette énigme, nous proposons que les effets de débordement et d’éviction du FDI puissent s’appliquer respectivement à différentes phases de l’innovation (c’est-à-dire la génération d’idées et la mise en œuvre de la R&D), ce qui conduit ensuite à des impacts différentiels du FDI sur l’innovation incrémentale et radicale. Appuyés sur un ensemble de données en panel d’entreprises chinoises cotées, nos résultats montrent que le FDI au niveau de l’industrie est positivement lié à l’innovation incrémentale, mais qu’il a un impact en forme de U inversé sur l’innovation radicale. En outre, nous constatons que l’écart technologique renforce l’impact positif du FDI sur l’innovation incrémentale tout en rendant son impact en forme de U inversé sur l’innovation radicale plus prononcé. De plus, lorsque le FDI est davantage axé sur le marché local, la relation en forme de U inversé entre le FDI et l’innovation radicale devient plus accentuée. Ces résultats réconcilient les incohérences concernant la manière dont le FDI peut affecter l’innovation locale, et fournissent un cadre d’analyse novateur pour la littérature du FDI. O investimento estrangeiro direto (FDI) interno promove ou inibe a inovação tecnológica de empresas locais? Pesquisas anteriores geraram diversas visões e achados sobre essa importante questão. Para abordar esse enigma, propomos que efeitos de transbordamento e de exclusão de FDI podem se aplicar a diferentes fases da inovação (ou seja, geração de ideias e implementação de R&D), o que por sua vez leva a impactos diferenciados do FDI na inovação incremental e radical. Os resultados de um conjunto de dados em painel de empresas chinesas listadas mostram que o FDI em nível de indústria está positivamente relacionado à inovação incremental, mas tem um impacto em forma de U invertido na inovação radical. Além disso, descobrimos que a lacuna tecnológica reforça o impacto positivo do FDI na inovação incremental, ao mesmo tempo que torna mais pronunciado o impacto em forma de U invertido na inovação radical, e que, quando o foco do mercado local do FDI é maior, a relação em forma de U invertido entre o FDI e a inovação radical é mais acentuada. Esses achados reconciliam a inconsistência sobre como o FDI pode afetar a inovação

Title: Foreignness as a double-edged sword for internationalizing cultural goods: deep learning–based semiotic analysis of Hollywood movies in China
Authors: Qian Cecilia Gu, Yanqing Wang, Jiamin Zhang
Abstract: La mondialisation des biens culturels s'est considérablement développée au cours de la dernière décennie. Enracinés dans le contexte social du pays d'origine, les biens culturels sont intrinsèquement << étrangers>> lorsqu'ils sont commercialisés dans un pays d'accueil. Restent néanmoins encore floues la manière dont l'extranéité se manifeste dans les biens culturels ainsi que la façon dont les handicaps et les avantages liés à l’extranéité (Liability and Asset of Foreignness) influencent conjointement leur performance sur le marché du pays d'accueil. Nous abordons ces questions en examinant 304 films hollywoodiens en Chine entre 2011 et 2018, en nous concentrant sur l'extranéité sémiotique - les différences entre les synopsis et les affiches des films hollywoodiens et chinois. Nous utilisons les représentations d'encodeur bidirectionnel à partir de réseaux auto-attentifs (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers - BERT) pour analyser les synopsis et la mesure de similarité structurelle (Structural Similarity Index Measure - SSIM) pour les affiches, ce qui nous permet de comprendre comment le public interprète et perçoit l'extranéité dans les textes et les images. Les résultats montrent une relation en forme de U inversé entre le caractère étranger de l'affiche et les ventes au box-office des films hollywoodiens en Chine, ce qui indique qu'un caractère étranger modéré de l'affiche entraîne des ventes optimales. En revanche, la performance du box-office est insensible à l'extranéité du synopsis. Notre recherche apporte des renseignements précieux sur les points de vue divergents concernant l'extranéité et son rôle dans les performances du pays d'accueil. Elle répond également aux critiques formulées à l'encontre du concept d'extranéité, mal opérationnalisé et spécifié, et constitue d’ailleurs une première tentative de rapprochement entre la littérature des affaires internationales et le caractère distinctif optimal. Cultural goods, like movies, play an important role in the global economy. These goods often come from different countries and bring unique cultural elements with them. When these cultural goods enter a new country, they can be seen as foreign, which affects how local people perceive them. This study looks at how Hollywood movies perform in China and how their "foreignness" impacts their success. The authors explore whether imitating local styles or maintaining a foreign appeal is better for these movies. This article examines Hollywood movies' success in China by analyzing their synopses (short summaries) and posters. The researchers used advanced technology, like deep learning (a type of artificial intelligence), to measure how different these elements are from local Chinese movies. They found that a moderate level of foreignness in movie posters leads to the best box office performance. This means that when posters are somewhat different but not too foreign, they attract more viewers. The study used data from 304 Hollywood movies released in China between 2011 and 2018, comparing them with local films to understand the impact of foreignness. The results show that movie posters with a moderate level of foreignness perform best in China. This suggests that while some foreign elements can make a movie appealing, too much can be off-putting. Interestingly, the synopses' level of foreignness did not significantly affect box office sales. The study concludes that balancing foreign and local elements is key to success in international markets. This research provides insights into how cultural products can be marketed globally and suggests that future studies could explore other cultural goods or consider geopolitical changes affecting consumer perceptions. Title: The internationalization of digital cultural content creators on global social media: navigating virtual outsidership in a borderless space
Authors: Rui Yang, Noman Shaheer, Yonggui Wang, Zhuyi Angelina Li
Abstract: Global social media (GSM) is reshaping cultural industries by enabling digital content creators to share their content with global audiences. The resulting surge in content heralds a new era of experience-based consumption, where multicultural audiences continually seek novel experiences and rapidly shift to content that aligns with their evolving interests. The dynamic landscape of GSM indicates a substantial gap in digital internationalization research that largely focuses on overcoming the liability of outsidership to acquire new users while neglecting the challenge of sustaining long-term audience engagement. We address this gap by highlighting the unique challenge of virtual outsidership, which refers to the difficulty of attracting and retaining viewership amid shifting audience preferences. Extending product innovation research, we propose that creators can mitigate virtual outsidership by consistently producing novel content, though its effectiveness varies in GSM’s multicultural landscape. Specifically, novel content is more effective when audience preferences across countries align but less effective when cultural content significantly differs across regions. A panel data analysis of 355 YouTube channels across 24 countries supports our arguments. Our study advances digital internationalization research by identifying unique challenges in digital cultural industries and proposing strategies to sustain audience engagement in GSM’s dynamic environment. Las redes sociales globales (GSM por sus iniciales en inglés) están transformando las industrias culturales al permitir que los creadores de contenido digital compartan su trabajo con audiencias globales. El consecuente aumento en el contenido anuncia una nueva era de consumo basado en experiencias, donde las audiencias multiculturales buscan continuamente experiencias novedosas y cambian rápidamente hacia contenidos que se alinean con sus intereses en evolución. El panorama dinámico de las redes sociales globales evidencia una brecha sustancial en la investigación sobre internacionalización digital, que se centra principalmente en superar la desventaja de estar en condición de “outsider” (liability of outsidership, LOO) para adquirir nuevos usuarios, mientras descuida el desafío de mantener el compromiso de la audiencia a largo plazo. Abordamos esta brecha destacando el desafío único de la condición de “outsider” virtual, que se refiere a la dificultad de atraer y retener espectadores en medio de preferencias cambiantes de la audiencia. Ampliando la investigación sobre innovación de productos, proponemos que los creadores pueden mitigar condición de “outsider” virtual mediante la producción constante de contenido novedoso, aunque su efectividad varía en el panorama multicultural de las redes sociales globales. Específicamente, el contenido novedoso es más efectivo cuando las preferencias de la audiencia entre países se alinean, pero menos efectivo cuando el contenido cultural difiere significativamente entre regiones. Un análisis de datos de panel de 355 canales de YouTube en 24 países respalda nuestros argumentos. Nuestro estudio avanza en la investigación sobre internacionalización digital al identificar desafíos únicos en las industrias culturales digitales y proponer estrategias para mantener el compromiso de la audiencia en el entorno dinámico de las redes sociales globales. 全球社交媒体 (GSM) 使数字内容创作者能够与全球受众分享其内容，从而重塑文化产业。由此产生的内容激增预示着基于体验消费的新时代的到来，多元文化的受众不断寻求新颖体验，并迅速转向符合他们不断变化的兴趣的内容。GSM 的动态格局表明数字国际化研究存在巨大空白，这些研究主要关注于克服局外人劣势(LOO) 来获得新用户，而忽视了维持长期受众参与的挑战。我们通过强调虚拟局外人的独特挑战来填补这一空白，这是指在观众偏好不断变化的情况下吸引和留住观众群的困难。我们扩展了产品创新研究，建议创作者通过持续制作新颖的内容来减轻虚拟局外人的影响，尽管其有效性在 GSM 的多元文化格局中有所不同。具体来说，当不同国家的受众偏好一致时，新颖的内容会更有效，但当不同地区的文化内容存在显著差异时，新颖内容的效果就会较差。对 24 个国家/地区 355 个 YouTube 频道的面板数据分析支持了我们的论点。我们的研究通过识别数字文化产业中的独特挑战并提出在 GSM 动态环境中维持受众参与的策略推进了数字国际化研究。 A mídia social global (GSM) está remodelando indústrias culturais, permitindo que criadores de conteúdo digital compartilhem seu conteúdo com uma aud

Title: A social influence view of the internationalization of cultural products
Authors: Xinli Huang, Di Fan, Christine Soo
Abstract: Abstract A thriving international cultural industry fuels the expansion of the global creative economy. Yet, what drives the international diffusion and performance of cultural products? This study adopts a social influence perspective to examine the international performance of film exports, addressing a critical gap in existing research that often isolates social influences without considering the impact of their (in)congruence. Given the subjective nature of cultural products and their vulnerability to multiple influences across global value chains, we theorize and empirically test the effects of congruence and incongruence between supply-side and demand-side social influences on films’ international performance. Analyzing 1676 U.S. films released between 2009 and 2018, our findings reveal that congruence between supply-side and demand-side social influences significantly enhances a film’s appeal, credibility, and international success. Moreover, this effect is amplified by two key moderators across global value chains, namely, upstream home-country adoption of social media promotion and downstream host-country press freedom. This study contributes to the understanding of the social influence view within global value chains by highlighting the importance of supply-demand congruence and the contextual factors that shape their effectiveness in driving the international performance of cultural products.

Title: Local roots, global reach? A framework for managing place-based identity in new cultural industries
Authors: Stephanie Wang, Marjorie A. Lyles, Allan Bird, Joseph Lampel
Abstract: Los productos culturales, caracterizados por una rica expresión artística y un significado simbólico, ahora se producen y distribuyen globalmente a una velocidad sin precedentes. Sin embargo, a medida que su alcance se expande, también lo hace la resistencia, ya que los bienes culturales se ven cada vez más enredados en tensiones geopolíticas, sensibilidades culturales y políticas de identidad. Esta paradoja, de un acceso global más fácil pero una aceptación local más disputada, plantea nuevos desafíos estratégicos para las empresas multinacionales (EMNs) en estas industrias y presenta valiosas oportunidades para que los académicos de negocios internacionales (IB, por sus siglas en inglés) revisen teorías fundamentales. En este artículo, revisamos la esencia de la cultura y las industrias culturales "clásicas", resumimos las fuerzas impulsoras de las "nuevas" industrias culturales y presentamos una tipología que explica las estrategias competitivas de las empresas en estas industrias que compiten a nivel global. Específicamente, proponemos un marco CASE (CAEE por las iniciales en español) que explica cómo las empresas pueden conectar, asimilar, exhibir y enriquecer su identidad basada en el lugar, dependiendo de si la autenticidad está vinculada a una ubicación o no, así como de si la extranjería se percibe como una desventaja o un activo. Finalmente, resumimos los seis artículos incluidos en este número especial y concluimos con orientaciones para futuras investigaciones. Les produits culturels — caractérisés par une riche expression artistique et une signification symbolique — sont désormais produits et distribués à l'échelle mondiale à une vitesse sans précédent. Pourtant, à mesure que leur portée s'élargit, la résistance augmente également, car les biens culturels deviennent de plus en plus imbriqués dans les tensions géopolitiques, les sensibilités culturelles et les politiques identitaires. Ce paradoxe - un accès mondial plus facile mais une acceptation locale plus contestée -pose de nouveaux défis stratégiques aux entreprises multinationales (Multinational Enterprises – MNEs) dans ces industries, et offre aux chercheurs en affaires internationales (International Business - IB) de précieuses opportunités pour revoir les théories fondamentales. Dans cet article, nous revisitons l'essence de la culture et des industries culturelles « classiques », résumons les forces motrices des « nouvelles » industries culturelles, et présentons une typologie expliquant les stratégies compétitives des entreprises dans ces industries qui se font concurrence à l'échelle mondiale. Plus précisément, nous proposons un cadre CASE qui explique comment les entreprises peuvent connecter, assimiler, mettre en valeur et enrichir leur identité locale, selon que l'authenticité est liée ou non à un lieu, et que l'étrangeté est perçue comme un handicap ou un atout. Enfin, nous résumons les six articles inclus dans ce numéro spécial, et concluons par des orientations pour les recherches futures. Produtos culturais — caracterizados por uma rica expressão artística e significado simbólico — são agora produzidos e distribuídos globalmente a uma velocidade sem precedentes. No entanto, à medida que seu alcance se expande, também cresce a resistência, já que os bens culturais se tornam cada vez mais entrelaçados com tensões geopolíticas, 43 sensibilidades culturais e políticas de identidade. Este paradoxo — acesso global mais fácil, mas aceitação local mais contestada — apresenta novos desafios estratégicos para empresas multinacionais (MNEs) nesses setores e oferece oportunidades valiosas para acadêmicos de negócios internacionais (IB) revisitarem teorias fundamentais. Neste artigo, revisitamos a essência da cultura e das indústrias culturais "clássicas", resumimos as forças motrizes das "novas" indústrias culturais e apresentamos uma tipologia que explica as estratégias competitivas de empresas nesses setores que competem globalmente.
