Navigating geopolitical risks: How U.S. firms adjust supply chains amid U.S.–China rivalry
Authors: Bo Yang, Jinyuan Song, Yifan Wei, Jing Li
Abstract: Investigamos como empresas norte-americanas adaptam suas cadeias de suprimento na China em resposta a riscos geopolíticos decorrentes da rivalidade entre os EUA e China. Oferecemos uma perspectiva de equilíbrio entre legitimidade e eficiência para entender decisões empresariais. Hipotetizamos que, para manter a legitimidade junto ao governo de origem, empresas norte-americanas em indústrias estratégicas têm maior probabilidade, em comparação com aquelas em indústrias não estratégicas, de alinhar-se à estratégia de mitigação de riscos do governo norte-americano, limitando fornecedores na China. No entanto, esperamos que essa tendência seja enfraquecida para empresas com alta dependência econômica da China. Analisando dados de fornecedores em nível empresarial de 2009 a 2022, descobrimos que a diferença no número de fornecedores chineses entre empresas estratégicas e não estratégicas dos EUA aumentou desde 2017 (primeira administração Trump). Empresas em indústrias estratégicas mantêm menos fornecedores chineses, refletindo potencialmente uma abordagem mais cautelosa. Essa disparidade era inicialmente mais pronunciada apenas entre empresas com inclinação republicana, mas posteriormente se estendeu a empresas de todo o espectro político sob a administração Biden. A diferença diminuiu entre empresas com maior dependência da China para receita ou suprimentos, sugerindo que considerações de eficiência podem atenuar a inclinação para alinhamento a estratégias nacionais. Dessa forma, empresas norte-americanas podem buscar equilibrar legitimidade política em seu país com benefícios econômicos derivados da China ao tomar decisões sobre fornecedores. The article explores how U.S. firms adjust their supply chains in response to geopolitical tensions, particularly between the U.S. and China. Geopolitical risks arise when home governments push firms to reduce reliance on rival countries, affecting their global operations. Since the first Trump administration in 2017, the U.S. government pressured U.S. firms to reduce their supply chains in China. Using detailed firms’ supplier data from 2009 to 2022, this study finds that while U.S. firms continued to expand their networks in China overall, those in strategic industries have 29% fewer Chinese suppliers compared to their counterparts in non-strategic industries since 2017, reflecting a cautious approach amid rising geopolitical risks. This disparity was initially more pronounced among Republican-leaning firms during the Trump administration but extended to all political leanings under the Biden administration, as Washington’s China strategy became more bipartisan. The study also finds that firms with significant revenue from China or limited alternative suppliers are less likely to reduce their Chinese suppliers, highlighting the trade-off between political legitimacy and economic efficiency. This study suggests that firms balance maintaining political legitimacy with economic benefits when navigating geopolitical risks. It advances understanding of how firms adapt their global strategies in response to geopolitical challenges. Title: Beyond words: the challenge of measuring financial text across borders
Abstract: Métodos baseados em dicionários são amplamente utilizados para avaliar o conteúdo informacional de comunicados ao mercado, mas foram desenvolvidos, em sua maioria, no contexto dos Estados Unidos. Este estudo aplica uma abordagem popular americana baseada em dicionário para analisar o sentimento dos comunicados em 200.960 transcrições de teleconferências de resultados em 85 países. Embora o sentimento dos comunicados esteja associado positivamente aos retornos acionários de curto prazo globalmente, essa relação é aproximadamente 30% mais fraca para empresas não norte-americanas. Com base na teoria contábil cultural, constatamos que diferenças culturais desempenham um papel central na explicação dessa disparidade. Em termos de implicações práticas, observamos que estratégias de investimento baseadas em sentimento são eficazes tanto para empresas norte-americanas quanto não norte-americanas que operam em ambientes culturalmente similares, mas não para empresas de países culturalmente distantes. Para tratar uma possível endogeneidade, utilizamos características linguísticas como variáveis instrumentais que refletem valores culturais históricos. Além disso, aplicamos um modelo de aprendizado de máquina treinado com dados norte-americanos, que continua a revelar limitações culturais quando utilizado internacionalmente. Nossos achados ressaltam a importância do contexto institucional e cultural na análise textual internacional e destacam as limitações da aplicação de métodos empíricos centrados nos Estados Unidos em escala global. O desenvolvimento de abordagens empíricas culturalmente sensíveis e contextualizadas tem potencial para aprimorar a mensuração e a compreensão da comunicação financeira em contextos internacionais. This article explores the challenges of using U.S.-centric methods for analyzing business communication in international contexts. Researchers often apply U.S. cultural values universally, which can lead to inaccuracies when studying non-U.S. settings. The study focuses on the limitations of using a U.S.-based textual analysis tool, the Loughran & McDonald (LM) dictionary, to measure sentiment in earnings conference calls from firms in 85 countries. The key finding is that the relationship between sentiment and market reactions is stronger for U.S. firms compared to non-U.S. firms, highlighting the need for culturally sensitive research methods. This article uses a dataset of 200,960 earnings conference call transcripts from 85 countries to investigate whether the LM dictionary can reliably capture disclosure sentiment internationally. The LM dictionary is a tool used to analyze financial sentiment by counting positive and negative words in texts. The study examines if the strength of the relationship between sentiment and market reactions varies across countries. It also explores whether investors can use sentiment measures to predict future stock returns. The analysis shows that U.S.-based sentiment measures work well for U.S. firms but not for non-U.S. firms. The study uses Gray’s cultural accounting framework to explain these findings, suggesting that cultural differences, such as individualism and uncertainty avoidance, affect how financial disclosures are interpreted. The results indicate that cultural distance from the U.S. significantly impacts the effectiveness of U.S.-centric sentiment measures. In culturally similar countries, the relationship between sentiment and market reactions is stronger, while it weakens in culturally distant countries. This study highlights the importance of considering cultural context in international business research. The findings suggest that researchers should develop culturally sensitive methods for analyzing business communication. Future research could focus on creating new tools that account for cultural differences, improving the accuracy of sentiment analysis in global contexts. Title: Reputational judgments of foreign MNEs’ societal impact in frontier markets: the role of compatible, crossed, and conflicting signals
Authors: Erin E. Makarius, Aloysius M. Kahindi, Charles E. Stevens, Emma Kyoungseo Hong
Abstract: Abstract How do host country stakeholders evaluate foreign MNEs’ local impact? Although MNEs’ desire for a reputation for positive societal impact is well-established in the literature, much less is known about how to actually obtain one—especially in less developed frontier markets. In this inductive, qualitative study across seven countries in sub-Saharan Africa, we examine why host country stakeholders deem some foreign MNEs to have a better reputation for societal impact than others and how firms’ actions and attributes influence these stakeholder perceptions. Leveraging signaling theory, we identify three distinct types of signals (compatible, crossed, and conflicting) and three critical factors (benefit diffusion, empowerment, and hybrid solutions) that shape MNEs’ reputation for societal impact. We also shed light on the role of contextual factors at the country, industry, and community levels. In addition to these theoretical contributions, our study also yields practical implications for MNEs of including local stakeholders’ perspectives when crafting market and nonmarket strategies, fostering constructive communication between headquarters and subsidiaries as well as between expatriate and local actors, and finding ways of going beyond ‘fitting in’ to instead ‘stand out’ in order to gain a reputation for providing tangible and intangible forms of societal impact in frontier markets.

Title: The effects of government debt on corporate borrowing in developing economies: evidence from Africa
Authors: Gonul Colak, Theogene Habimana, Timo Korkeamäki
Abstract: Abstract Many African economies face high debt levels, yet local firms have unique growth opportunities requiring external financing. We examine whether government borrowing constrains corporate financing in Africa and how these effects differ by debt source. Using a manually collected dataset from 29 African countries (2000–2019), we uncover financing patterns that challenge conventional theories. In sharp contrast to firms in developed markets, we find that African firms experience a “crowding-in” effect when governments borrow externally, enhancing their access to debt. In contrast, domestic government borrowing induces the typical crowding-out effect, where government borrowing reduces corporate access to debt. The crowding-in phenomenon is most evident among publicly listed firms, particularly those cross-listed on foreign exchanges (the multinationals). The effect strengthens in countries with higher Eurobond market activity and intensifies following sovereign credit downgrades, underscoring the sovereign ceiling’s constraint on corporate borrowing. Our findings contribute significantly to international business literature by revealing how African debt markets function differently, highlighting unique financing challenges faced by African multinational enterprises, and demonstrating that economic principles established in developed markets cannot be universally applied to emerging economies. These insights are crucial for designing effective policies to support corporate growth in Africa.

Title: Privacy protection laws, national culture, and artificial intelligence innovation around the world
Authors: Hyungseok David Yoon, Mustapha Belkhouja, Luis Alfonso Dau
Abstract: Abstract A substantial body of research highlights how stringent regulations disrupt innovators’ incentives and increase transaction costs, yet their information processing implication remains understudied. Building on information processing theory, we study how the interplay between formal and informal institutions shapes inventors’ information processing in developing artificial intelligence (AI) innovation. We examine the effect of stringent privacy regulations on AI innovation by exploiting the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) announcement. We argue that, following the GDPR announcement, GDPR-affected countries experience lower national AI innovation rates than unaffected countries. Further, we postulate that this negative effect is weaker in GDPR-affected countries, marked by higher levels of individualism, masculinity, and indulgence, but stronger in the affected countries with higher levels of uncertainty avoidance, power distance, and long-term orientation. Our difference-in-differences analysis supports the proposed framework. Our research contributes to the international business literature by developing novel theoretical predictions at the intersection of comparative institutional analysis and national culture, explaining how privacy protection laws and cultural factors shape AI inventors’ information processing. Finally, this study provides insights into how inventors and entrepreneurs in countries with stringent privacy laws can leverage national culture to shape their AI innovation strategies and inform strategic decision-making.

Title: Translation of equality, diversity, and inclusion ideas in a foreign subsidiary
Authors: Cristina Leone, Arabella Mocciaro Li Destri, Pasquale Massimo Picone
Abstract: Abstract Drawing on a sociological approach, this paper examines how the subsidiaries of multinational companies (MNCs) translate equality, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) ideas from their headquarters (HQs). International business (IB) studies emphasize the context-sensitive and socially constructed nature of EDI. Through a single case study of an Italian subsidiary translating EDI ideas from its U.S. HQs, we present a power-laden EDI translation process and broaden the extant research by revealing the power relations underlying the EDI translation process. We portray the sociology of MNCs in which different professional categories engage in “translation spaces”, i.e., social spaces where they interact throughout various phases of the translation process. Specifically, we identify two key phases: the signification and negotiation phases. In these phases, intentional and unintentional translators play varying roles in either facilitating or hindering the translation of EDI ideas within the subsidiary. Thus, we first advance the sociology of EDI translation in IB by revealing how EDI understanding is constructed and reconstructed through the interactions of translators. Second, we contribute to translation research in IB by depicting the iterative and recursive nature of the translation process. Finally, we reveal forms of resistance to EDI and the emergence of new power relations shaped by professional diversity within the subsidiary, unearthing the generative nature of the EDI translation process in MNCs.

Title: Small worlds within global supply chains: implications for multinational enterprises’ environmental, social, and governance controversies
Authors: Sangho Chae, Igor Filatotchev, Seongtae Kim, Byung-Gak Son
Abstract: Abstract With increasing public attention to corporate sustainability, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) controversies emerging in global supply chains present a growing problem for multinational enterprises (MNEs). This paper investigates whether MNEs with geographically dispersed suppliers are more likely to be exposed to supplier-related ESG controversies. It also explores structural characteristics of global supply chains that can mitigate MNEs’ exposure to such controversies. Building on the literature on supply chain complexity and small-world networks, we suggest that the small-worldness of an MNE’s supply chain network can mitigate the impact of the geographical dispersion of suppliers on supplier-induced ESG controversies. Our analysis of the Fortune 500 largest U.S. companies from 2010 to 2019 reveals that MNEs with geographically dispersed suppliers suffer from more supplier-induced ESG controversies, while small-worldness attenuates such impact. Our findings contribute to the international business literature by highlighting small-worldness as a network structural characteristic that can be deployed by MNEs to mitigate the negative impacts of supply chain spatial complexity.

Title: Beyond reductionism: rethinking MNEs’ role in environmental crises
Authors: Liena Kano, Birgitte Grøgaard, Luciano Ciravegna, Gilbert Kofi Adarkwah
Abstract: Abstract This counterpoint challenges the view advanced by Yu, Bansal, and Arjaliès (J Int Business Stud 54:1151–1169, 2023), who argue that multinational enterprises (MNEs), by virtue of their cross-border operations, are inherently detrimental to the environment. While Yu et al.’s call for responsible resource use is commendable, we contend that their framework oversimplifies the complex realities of international business (IB). Drawing on New Internalization Theory (NIT), we examine environmental crises through the lens of multilevel complexity—macro-level institutional interdependencies, firm-level heterogeneity, and individual-level cognitive and behavioral constraints. Our approach underscores the role of bounded rationality and bounded reliability across all relevant actors—not just MNE managers—in shaping environmental outcomes. We find that Yu et al.’s proposed strategies give limited attention to the institutional, industry, organizational, and governance conditions under which environmental value is created. By contrast, we apply comparative institutional analysis to investigate MNEs’ impact on the environment as compared to feasible, real-world alternatives. We argue that meaningful environmental progress hinges not on targeting MNEs, but on fostering multilateral coordination among public, private, and civil society actors, with MNEs being well positioned to lead such collaborations. We call for scholarship that avoids ideological overreach, embraces IB theory, and acknowledges MNEs as key agents in advancing environmental sustainability.

Title: Venture capital funding in Africa: a mixed-methods study of evolving ecosystems and financial discrimination
Abstract: Abstract Africa’s startup ecosystem is growing rapidly, yet venture capital (VC) funding remains disproportionately allocated to non-African founders. This study investigates the factors driving this disparity, focusing on institutional voids – gaps in legal frameworks, financial infrastructure, and market-supporting institutions – and investors’ perceptions of risk and financial discrimination. We conducted 37 interviews with investors and entrepreneurs to identify the determinants of VC funding, including startup location, founder origin, and international networks. Additionally, a qualitative comparative analysis of 335 African fintech startups revealed the factor configurations that enable startups to secure high levels of VC investment. Historically, the findings reveal that non-African founders have benefited from investor homophily, a preference for investing in individuals with similar backgrounds, to mitigate the perceived risks related to institutional voids. By contrast, African founders faced greater barriers to funding. However, as Africa’s VC ecosystem has matured, local founders have begun to overcome these obstacles. By linking institutional voids to homophily and embedding a postcolonial perspective, acknowledging how historical power dynamics and colonial legacies shape investor perceptions and market structures, this study sheds light on the systemic biases that shape VC funding. These findings offer actionable insights for investors, policymakers, and entrepreneurs aiming to foster a more inclusive VC landscape.

Title: Heterogeneity and internationalization of government investments: sovereign wealth funds and beyond
Abstract: Government investment funds (GIFs), such as sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) and public pension funds (PFs), are major players in global finance. They manage vast resources and sometimes pursue political goals. This study explores how these funds invest and the impact on the companies they target. The authors aim to understand the differences between GIFs and private investors, focusing on the types of companies they invest in and the returns generated. This article examines 392 investments by 129 government-owned funds, including SWFs, public pension funds, and their subsidiaries, from 1983 to 2023. It compares these to 67,072 investments by private firms. The study finds that GIFs often target large, foreign companies and prefer smaller ownership stakes. They are more active during financial crises and when monetary policies are restrictive in their home countries. The research uses event-study analysis to assess market reactions to GIF investments, finding that GIFs generally generate lower returns for target companies compared to private investors. However, subsidiaries of GIFs, known as sovereign wealth enterprises (SWEs), tend to achieve higher returns, especially when investing domestically. The results show that GIFs differ from private investors in their investment strategies and outcomes. SWFs and public pension funds often generate lower returns, possibly due to political influences and less efficient management. In contrast, SWEs, which operate more independently, achieve better results. The study suggests that GIFs are not solely focused on economic goals but also pursue political and social objectives. This research highlights the need for GIFs to clarify their goals and improve governance to enhance their effectiveness. Future implications include the potential for GIFs to play a significant role in international finance, especially during periods of economic uncertainty. Despite its continued significance and dynamic forms, government ownership is often presented in broad, monolithic terms. Comparing 67,464 government and private acquirer transactions over four decades, we highlight important distinctions in target selection and valuation effects of 129 unique government investment funds (GIFs), including sovereign wealth funds (SWFs), lesser-known subsidiaries called sovereign wealth enterprises (SWEs), and government-owned pension funds. GIFs, particularly SWFs, are significantly more likely to make foreign investments than non-government investors, which is consistent with their pursuit of internationalization. However, GIFs purchase smaller stakes in targets compared to private acquirers, reflecting concerns about their legitimacy and control over businesses, especially in foreign SWE transactions. Considering how investors evaluate government and private investments, we find that GIF transactions result in significantly lower target returns, with SWE acquisitions being the exception. Evidence suggests these results are driven by liabilities of stateness, such as multi-layered agency concerns and acquirer opaqueness, which vary across GIFs. We also find that macroeconomic conditions that restrict private investment create an internationalization channel for state investors. By recognizing a richer set of motivations and outcomes for various GIFs, public and private stakeholders can optimize state investment transactions, particularly as governments expand their use of different investing vehicles. 尽管政府所有权具有持续的重要性和动态式， 它常常以广义的、整体的术语呈现。 通过比较过去 40 年中的 67,464 笔政府和私人收购方的交易， 我们强调了 129 个独特的政府投资基金 (GIF) 在目标选择和估值效应方面的重要区别， 其中包括主权财富基金 (SWF)、称为主权财富企业 (SWE) 的鲜为人知的子公司以及政府拥有的养老基金。 GIF， 特别是SWF， 比非政府投资者更有可能进行外国投资， 这与它们的国际化追求是一致的。然而， 与私人收购方相比， GIF 购买的目标股份较少， 这反映出对其合法性和对企业的控制力的担忧， 尤其是在外国SWE交易中。考虑到投资者如何评估政府和私人投资， 我们发现 GIF 交易导致目标回报率显著降低， SWE 收购是个例外。 有证据表明， 这些结果是由国家责任驱动的， 例如多层的机构考虑和收购方的不透明性， 这在不同的 GIF 中有所不同。们还发现， 限制私人投资的宏观经济条件为国家投资者开辟了国际化渠道。通过认识各种 GIF 的更丰富的动机和结果， 公共和私人利益相关者可以优化国家投资交易， 特别是当政府扩大对不同投资工具的使用时。 Mesmo com sua importância

Title: Revisiting the liability of foreignness: political ideology, globalization, and discrimination
Authors: Yulia Muratova, Charles Dhanaraj, Liudmyla Svystunova
Abstract: Abstract Equal treatment of foreign and local firms is the cornerstone of international investment law. Yet, why do foreign firms face discrimination in host countries? We analyze this critical but underexplored aspect of the liability of foreignness in two stages. First, drawing on the insights from political science, we argue that the political ideology of the host government along the left-right spectrum drives discriminatory dynamics, resulting in elevated regulatory risk for foreign firms. Next, we argue that globalization moderates the relative regulatory risk while distinguishing political and social dimensions of globalization: political globalization amplifies the effect of ideology on discrimination, while social globalization mitigates it. We validate our theory using tax inspection data on 38,326 firms across 95 countries from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys between 2008 and 2019. We identify a novel, context-specific source of discrimination revealing how political ideology and globalization jointly shape the regulatory risk of foreign firms. We advance a growing stream of research that explores how political ideologies shape international business. CEOs must recognize that political ideology can drive discrimination risk and that globalization is a double-edged sword. Strategic planning demands nuanced integration of both factors to successfully mitigate discrimination in international markets.

Title: Indigenous peoples’ reactions to foreign direct investment: a social movement perspective
Authors: Anne Spencer Jamison, Doron Tadmor, Witold Jerzy Henisz
Abstract: Abstract A growing body of literature highlights that large-scale investments in sensitive contexts can undermine both firm financial performance and peace-positive development. We investigate whether and under what conditions foreign direct investment (FDI) proximate to Indigenous land claims increases or decreases conflict. Drawing on social movement theory’s identification of powerful frames and political opportunity structures as drivers of mobilization, we predict that FDI proximate to Indigenous land claims will promote conflict. We leverage novel data on the global location of Indigenous land claims and a global corpus of more than 4 billion news articles. We find that when locations with Indigenous land claims are treated with FDI, we observe an increase in media-reported armed conflict events. We further argue and find this effect to be driven by rebels acting on behalf of Indigenous people who target (multinational) corporations and the governments who offer them the formal license to operate. These negative effects are found across a wide range of industries. Our results underscore that for investments in sensitive socio-political contexts, such as Indigenous lands, firm performance and the livelihoods of community members are heavily influenced by conflict risk mitigation efforts.

Title: Global virtual work: a review, integrative framework, and future research opportunities
Authors: Fabian Jintae Froese, Tobias Blay, Cristina B. Gibson, Margaret A. Shaffer, Jose Benitez
Abstract: Abstract Digitalization and global disruptions have fundamentally changed how we approach work. Global virtual work has become increasingly widespread in recent years, often replacing or complementing traditional expatriation and international business travel. To advance our understanding of this phenomenon, we systematically reviewed the literature on global virtual work, distinguishing it into three domains: global virtual teams, distributed work, and the use of digital technologies. For each domain, we examined key actors, their objectives, underlying theories, methodologies, and findings. The first domain provides insights into the antecedents, moderators, and mediators of the effectiveness of global virtual teams. The second domain explores individual and organizational research on diverse distributed work arrangements, such as offshoring, global platforms, and global nomads. The third domain addresses the enabling and moderating roles that digital technologies play in facilitating global virtual work. Synthesizing prior research, we developed a multilevel conceptual framework that integrates inputs, processes, and outcomes of global virtual work, offering novel perspectives. We outlined promising opportunities for future research across four themes: people, technology, context, and time. Additionally, we examined the practical implications of our findings for policymakers, managers, and individual workers as they navigate the evolving landscape of global virtual work.

Title: The world for sale: money, power and the traders who barter the Earth’s resources
Oasis in the desert or icing on the cake? The impact of entrepreneurship accelerators across ecosystems
Abstract: Abstract The effectiveness of accelerators in fostering new venture development has traditionally been attributed to variations in their internal operations and design, with limited consideration of contextual factors. This study broadens the understanding of accelerators by situating their roles in relation to entrepreneurial ecosystems and introducing a multi-level framework on how macro-level institutions and meso-level accelerator programs interact to shape venture growth. By linking organizational theories on accelerators with institutional economics, this research juxtaposes and tests two perspectives: institutional voids and institutional support. On the one hand, accelerators address institutional voids by acting as intermediaries in entrepreneurial resource markets through knowledge and resource curation, network brokerage, and signaling. On the other hand, the effectiveness of these intermediation roles is constrained by the quality of institutions. Contrary to the prevailing belief that accelerators deliver greater value in underdeveloped institutional environments with inefficient entrepreneurial resource markets, the findings reveal that ventures in such contexts derive less growth benefit from accelerators. This study contributes to the growing body of comparative and international accelerator research and offers broader implications for meso-level intervention programs, suggesting these programs require working in concert with robust ecosystems rather than operating in isolation in order to achieve their intended objectives.

Title: Proactive investments in switching-flexibility and the value of agility in international business
Abstract: Como uma empresa multinacional (MNE) deve moldar sua própria agilidade em resposta aos ambientes em que opera? Neste artigo, argumentamos que investimentos proativos em flexibilidade de mudança, por exemplo, para facilitar futuras realocações de ativos de produção, podem ser uma ferramenta poderosa para lidar com a volatilidade de negócios internacionais (IB). Se opções para investir em flexibilidade futura forem exercidas de forma estratégica, a realocação internacional pode se tornar um fenômeno mais frequente em indústrias de alta volatilidade do que em indústrias de baixa volatilidade. Essa previsão contrasta com a recomendação do valor de espera da clássica literatura de opções reais, que sugere que a realocação se torna menos frequente quando a volatilidade é alta. As diferenças em previsões decorrem de uma mudança de perspectiva - de flexibilidade exógena na literatura clássica para a flexibilidade endógena neste estudo. Investimentos proativos ideais em agilidade futura aumentam o valor de uma firma e ampliam sua capacidade de lidar com riscos. Isso sugere que MNEs que operam em mercados internacionais voláteis e competitivos geralmente se tornam mais ágeis do que firma operando em ambientes estáveis. A proposição do artigo é apoiada por casos ilustrativos de indústrias oceânicas e por um modelo de opções reais com reversibilidade endógena. O modelo mostra que investimentos proativos ideais em flexibilidade podem restringir a diferença entre o limite de entrada e saída para maior volatilidade. In 2012, Viking River Cruises launched a new type of cruise ship called the Longship Class. These ships were designed to easily move between different river systems, making them flexible and adaptable to changing market conditions. This paper explores two main ideas: how investing in flexibility during the design phase can help businesses adapt to market changes, and how relocating production assets can be a successful international business strategy. The study aims to fill a gap in understanding how companies can enhance their agility and adaptability in unpredictable global markets. This article introduces a theoretical model that explains how proactive investments in flexibility can help businesses relocate their production assets more easily. The model is inspired by examples from the ocean and waterway industries, like Viking River Cruises, which show how initial investments in flexibility can make future relocations easier and less costly. The study uses a mathematical approach to demonstrate that investing in flexibility can reduce the costs associated with moving production assets between markets. This is particularly important in industries with high volatility, where market conditions change frequently. The model suggests that companies can benefit from making strategic investments early on to increase their ability to switch locations as needed. The study finds that proactive investments in flexibility can significantly enhance a company's ability to adapt to changing market conditions. By reducing the costs of relocating production assets, these investments make it easier for companies to enter and exit markets as needed. This approach is especially valuable in volatile industries, where market conditions are unpredictable. The research contributes to existing literature by highlighting the importance of flexibility in international business strategies. In the future, companies that invest in flexibility may be better positioned to respond quickly to market changes, giving them a competitive edge in global markets. Title: Rethinking international business scholarship as cross-language knowledge production: a dialogical approach to qualitative research
Abstract: Abstract As a disciplinary field, international business (IB) is characterized by language diversity. Too often, however, international business (IB) research regards language diversity as a challenge to be overcome rather than an opportunity to generate new scientific knowledge. Consequently, previous research has primarily focused on the pragmatic, logistical, and methodological hurdles of translating multilingual datasets. In contrast, this conceptual paper takes language diversity as an opportunity to produce new knowledge and proposes a dialogical approach to qualitative cross-language research. The dialogical approach has the potential to enrich IB research with novel perspectives from under-represented voices, improve the understanding of IB phenomena and nurture tolerance for diversity and inclusion through cross-language interaction. It is worth noting that the dialogical approach does not promote shared understanding but mutual understanding that is achieved through collaboration. In doing so, it builds on two types of dialogue: (self-)reflexive dialogue, and dialogue between the researcher and others (interviewees, supervisors, and collaborators participating in the research process). The outcome is knowledge that is pluralistic and multivocal, including the voices that belong to non-English-speaking participants and scholars. We argue that the dialogical approach contributes to the future vision of responsible and linguistically inclusive IB scholarship.

Title: Holding back the damage: strong political institutions and the effect of populism on business investment
Authors: Margherita Corina, Christopher Hartwell, Alfonso Carballo
Abstract: Abstract Populism is a political phenomenon that attempts to harness existing institutions for populist ends, often leading to negative consequences for businesses. However, can national institutions resist this pressure and mitigate the damage to firms? This paper investigates how populist electoral success influences corporate investment, unraveling the intricate connection between a country’s political institutions and the investment behavior of companies. Through the lens of political uncertainty and transaction cost economics, we theorize that countries with fortified checks and balances—facilitated by electoral systems (situated at the entrance to power), judicial independence (supervising the exercise of power), and government accountability (serving as ex-post checks)—effectively mitigate populist impulses. However, these checks and balances are also often targeted by populist leaders, as they prevent full implementation of a populist agenda. Analyzing a dataset spanning over 36,000 firms across 42 countries from 1995 to 2021, we find that existing checks and balances shield firms from populist excesses. In line with our theory, the longer a ruler is in power, the weaker these checks and balances remain. Our study highlights populism’s harm to business and the role of robust political institutions as mitigating factors.

Title: Forging agents of the state? How political institutions impact CEO compensation in state-owned enterprises
Authors: Roxana Turturea, Steve Sauerwald, Pursey P. M. A. R. Heugens
Abstract: Los gobiernos de todo el mundo utilizan la compensación ejecutiva para vincular a los CEO de empresas estatales con agendas políticas a expensas de los propietarios privados. Extendemos la teoría de agencia principal–principal (PP) para profundizar en el comportamiento de cooptación de CEO por parte de los gobiernos. Primero, basándonos en la perspectiva institucional, teorizamos que las instituciones políticas moldean la capacidad de los gobiernos para desencadenar conflictos PP mediante la vinculación de los CEO de empresas estatales a través de la compensación ejecutiva. Segundo, aprovechando la literatura sobre capitalismo estatal comparado, conjeturamos que los CEO de empresas estatales vinculados mediante compensación apoyan estrategias alineadas con los objetivos estatales. La evidencia de muestras pareadas que abarca empresas que cotizan en bolsa de 20 países corrobora nuestras predicciones. El efecto de la propiedad estatal sobre la compensación de los CEO varía sustancialmente entre países, y esta variación se explica en parte por la heterogeneidad en las instituciones políticas. Más específicamente, encontramos que los CEO de empresas estatales gozan de mayor compensación en contextos caracterizados por alto poder político y faccionalización política, y baja polarización política y restricción política. También encontramos que los CEO de empresas estatales mejor remunerados apoyan niveles excesivos de empleo y desempeño social corporativo, estrategias alineadas con los objetivos estatales. En general, demostramos que la compensación de los CEO es una herramienta destacada y efectiva utilizada por los gobiernos para convertir a los CEO de empresas estatales en agentes del Estado. State-owned enterprises (SOEs) are companies where the government owns a significant share. These companies often have both public and private ownership, making them "hybrid" SOEs. Governments sometimes use these companies to achieve political goals, like creating jobs or improving social conditions, which can conflict with the interests of private shareholders. This study explores how governments might use CEO compensation (the pay and benefits given to chief executive officers) to align CEOs with government goals, potentially at the expense of private shareholders. This article examines data from publicly listed firms in 20 countries between 2011 and 2016. It investigates how political institutions – like political power (government's influence in parliament), political factionalization (divisions within state institutions), political polarization (ideological differences between ruling and opposition parties), and political constraint (checks and balances on government decisions) – affect the relationship between state ownership and CEO compensation. The study also looks at whether CEO compensation influences SOE strategies, particularly in terms of employment levels and corporate social performance (CSP, which includes environmental and social initiatives). The findings suggest that CEO compensation is generally lower in SOEs than in private firms. However, political institutions play a significant role in this dynamic. For instance, when governments have more power or when there is high factionalization, they are more likely to use CEO compensation to bond CEOs to their political agendas. Conversely, high political polarization and constraint tend to reduce CEO compensation in SOEs. The study also finds that well-compensated CEOs in SOEs are more likely to support government goals like excess employment and CSP. This research highlights how governments can use CEO pay as a tool to influence company strategies in line with political objectives. In the future, understanding these dynamics could help balance government goals with shareholder interests in hybrid SOEs. Title: Space: a new frontier for international business
Authors: Arpit Raswant, Bo Bernhard Nielsen, Peter J. Buckley
Abstract: Abstract This article examines (outer) Space as a new frontier for international business (IB) and highlights the unique challenges and opportunities it presents. Unlike terrestrial business environments, Space is characterized by extreme physical conditions, ambiguous property rights, and an institutional vacuum, which disrupt conventional IB theories. The study identifies three key challenges—congestion, contention, and competition—arising from the commercialization of Space and the increasing presence of multinational enterprises (MNEs) in the sector. Utilizing the OLI (ownership, location, internalization) framework, the paper critically reassesses existing IB theories, considering these Space-specific complexities and their long-term implications for global business strategy. Furthermore, it explores the geopolitical and regulatory implications of Space activities, arguing that the absence of effective governance structures necessitates novel policy frameworks and cooperative mechanisms to ensure responsible expansion. The study also underscores the role of MNEs in shaping sustainable Space commercialization, proposing the addition of a new 18th Sustainable Development Goal—Sustainable Space. The findings contribute to IB scholarship by advancing theoretical approaches that account for the spatial, institutional, and competitive dynamics unique to (outer) Space, offering a foundation for future research, policy development, and industry collaboration in the era of Space-based business and security expansion.

Title: Taking a stand while abroad? Towards a theory of MNCs’ sociopolitical activism in host countries
Abstract: Les entreprises multinationales (Multinational Corporations - MNCs) prenant de plus en plus souvent position publiquement sur des questions sociopolitiques telles que l'immigration, les droits des LGBTQ+ et le racisme, il est impératif que la recherche en affaires internationales (International Business - IB) suive le rythme des débats sociétaux normatifs. Dans cet article, nous introduisons le concept d'activisme sociopolitique des entreprises (Corporate Sociopolitical Activism - SPA) dans la littérature de l’IB, et développons une théorie sur les raisons pour lesquelles les MNCs s'engagent de manière cohérente ou non dans le SPA en réponse à la même question dans leur pays d'origine et dans un pays d'accueil. Nous théorisons que la complexité institutionnelle à trois niveaux d'analyse - à l'intérieur d'un pays d'accueil, entre le pays d'origine et le pays d'accueil, et au-delà du pays d'origine et du pays d'accueil - façonne les décisions des MNCs. Cet article contribue à la littérature de l'IB en situant le SPA comme un nouveau domaine dans la recherche en stratégies internationales non marchandes. En outre, nous étendons la recherche en IB portée sur la complexité institutionnelle en théorisant la manière dont l'hétérogénéité au sein d'un pays d'accueil influence les comportements des MNCs. Nous élargissons également le champ d'investigation de la littérature du SPA en passant des entreprises domestiques aux MNCs. Dans l'ensemble, cet article constitue un appel à l'action pour les chercheurs en IB, qui doivent examiner les réponses des MNCs aux questions sociopolitiques dans un monde de plus en plus polarisé. 随着跨国公司 (MNC) 越来越多地在移民、LGBTQ+权利, 以及种族主义等社会政治问题上公开表明立场, 国际商务 (IB) 研究必须跟上规范性社会辩论的步伐。在本文中, 我们将企业社会政治行动主义 (SPA) 的概念引入 国际商务(IB) 文献中, 并发展了关于MNC为何一致或不一致地参与 SPA 的理论, 以应对母国和东道国的同一问题。我们认为, 东道国内部、母国与东道国之间以及母国与东道国之外三个分析层面的制度复杂性影响MNC的决策。本文通过将 SPA 定位为国际非市场战略研究中的一个新领域, 为 IB 文献做出了贡献。此外, 我们通过对东道国内部的异质性如何影响MNC行为的理论化, 扩展了关于制度复杂性的IB研究。我们还将企业 SPA 文献的重点从国内企业扩大到MNC。总体而言, 本文呼吁IB研究人员采取行动, 研究MNC在日益两极分化的世界中对社会政治问题的反应。 In recent years, multinational corporations (MNCs) have been increasingly involved in sociopolitical activism (SPA), which means publicly supporting or opposing social and political issues. However, these companies often show inconsistency in their actions across different countries. For example, some MNCs that supported racial justice in the U.S. did not take similar actions in Brazil. This inconsistency has led to criticism and calls for research to understand why MNCs behave this way. This article explores why MNCs might act consistently or inconsistently on the same sociopolitical issues in different countries. The authors propose a theory based on organizational values and institutional complexity. They argue that MNCs are likely to act consistently if they have already engaged in SPA in their home country because these actions reflect their core values. However, the complexity of operating in multiple countries, each with its own cultural norms and political environments, can influence their decisions. The article examines factors such as the level of agreement on an issue within a host country, differences between home and host countries, and pressures from international organizations. The findings suggest that MNCs are more likely to act consistently when their values align with those of the host country or when there is pressure from international bodies. However, significant cultural or regulatory differences between countries can lead to inconsistent actions. The authors conclude that understanding these dynamics can help predict MNCs’ behavior on global issues. This research contributes to the field by highlighting the importance of considering both internal values and external pressures when studying corporate activism. Future implications include guiding MNCs in navigating complex international environments and encouraging consistent engagement in sociopolitical issues worldwide. Title: Multinational enterprises and climate action: a low-income perspective with Africa focus
Abstract: Empresas multinacionais (MNEs) podem ser agentes de positiva ação climática por meio da utilização de seus vastos recursos, tecnologia, capital e parcerias colaborativas. Elas podem também promover a mobilidade transfronteiras de padrões regulatórios e de governança. Allen et al. (2024) fornecem uma análise descritiva sistemática para apoiar esse papel de MNEs. Em meu comentário, forneço uma perspectiva de países de baixa renda, particularmente da África. Embora enfrentem um impacto climático desproporcional, essas economias possuem recursos abundantes de energia limpa. Discuto o potencial de MNEs para ajudar a liberar o valor associado a esses recursos. Do lado do financiamento, bancos de MNEs podem disponibilizar sua tecnologia e recursos para promover empresas startups de financiamento climático. Eles também podem desempenhar um papel em parcerias público-privadas para liberar capital privado em escala para países de baixa renda. Allen et al. enfocam o lado positivo de MNEs na ação climática. Eu expando meu comentário para fornecer uma visão equilibrada e discutir o lado sombrio com foco na África. Destaco em particular o papel de bancos de MNEs na rápida acumulação da dívida soberana e nas dificuldades na reestruturação da dívida. Além disso, discuto o papel de MNEs na fuga de capitais. Resoluções bem-sucedidas para o superendividamento e redução da fuga de capitais podem liberar recursos para financiamento verde. Multinational enterprises (MNEs) are large companies that operate in multiple countries. They have significant resources and influence, which can be used for both positive and negative impacts on the environment. This article by Allen, Barbalau, Chavez, and Zeni explores how MNEs can play a positive role in addressing climate change. The authors highlight the potential of MNEs to use their size, resources, technology, and global reach to promote sustainable practices and reduce carbon emissions. They also discuss the importance of providing incentives to encourage MNEs to focus on climate-friendly actions. This article examines how MNEs can leverage their resources to support climate action. The authors use various examples and data to illustrate their points. They discuss how MNEs can use their supply chains to promote sustainable practices among suppliers. The article also explores the role of corporate governance (the system by which companies are directed and controlled) in encouraging MNEs to adopt environmentally friendly practices. The authors suggest that incentives like carbon taxes (a tax on carbon emissions) and green subsidies (financial support for environmentally friendly projects) can motivate MNEs to reduce their environmental impact. They also highlight the potential of green bonds (debt securities issued to fund projects with environmental benefits) as a tool for financing sustainable initiatives. The findings suggest that MNEs have the potential to be powerful agents of positive change in the fight against climate change. By using their resources and influence, they can help bridge the gap between private interests and social benefits. The authors conclude that while MNEs can contribute significantly to climate solutions, they need proper incentives to align their goals with societal needs. In the future, MNEs could play a crucial role in developing green economies, especially in low-income countries that are disproportionately affected by climate change. This could lead to more sustainable development and help address global environmental challenges. Title: Leveraging the capabilities of multinational firms to address climate change: a finance perspective
Authors: Franklin Allen, Adelina Barbalau, Erik Chavez, Federica Zeni
Abstract: Abstract Climate change and the associated issue of curbing carbon emissions have risen on the agenda of policymakers worldwide. However, global coordination on matters such as harmonized regulation has been subject to significant political frictions, and the large intergovernmental transfers needed to finance the transition of developing economies have proven hard to raise. Recently, there have been considerable responses to climate change from the private sector, with stakeholders placing more pressure on firms, and financial markets mobilizing increasingly more capital towards the reduction of negative externalities. We argue that although multinational enterprises (MNEs) have been a major contributor to the problem, they can be an important part of the solution – they have unique features that enable them to play an important role in the fight against climate change. MNEs have extensive and efficient internal markets for governance, financing, and technology, which enable them to circumvent country-specific frictions to climate action such as heterogeneous regulation, corruption, and the lack of technology. We analyze how different public and private incentive mechanisms could be designed to leverage MNEs’ unique features, realign their incentives, and engage their potential to play a role in decarbonizing the economy. Lastly, we discuss challenges, opportunities, and future research.

Title: Liability of foreignness in immersive technologies: evidence from extended reality innovations
Authors: Hyoryung Nam, Yiling Li, P. K. Kannan, Jeonghye Choi
Abstract: Les technologies émergentes de réalité étendue (Extended Reality - XR), telles que la réalité augmentée (Augmented Reality - AR) et la réalité virtuelle (Virtual Reality - VR), permettent aux entreprises internationales d'offrir des expériences immersives à leurs clients au-delà des frontières géographiques. Malgré les opportunités qu'elles offrent, l'exploitation des innovations de XR sur les marchés étrangers peut présenter des défis importants. La présente recherche examine si et dans quelles conditions les entreprises internationales sont confrontées aux handicaps et coûts liés à leur nationalité étrangère (Liability of Foreignness - LOF) lorsqu'elles tirent parti des innovations de XR. Nous argumentons que les LOF dans les innovations de XR découlent des désavantages inhérents auxquels les entreprises étrangères sont confrontées lorsqu'il s'agit de fournir des expériences de XR mentalement fluides, ce qui peut à son tour diminuer l'efficacité de leurs innovations de XR par rapport à leurs homologues locaux. Nous argumentons en outre que l'ampleur des LOF dans les innovations de XR varie en fonction des caractéristiques de la technologie de XR, avec les LOF plus importants dans les innovations de XR moins réalistes, plus interactives et plus vivantes. Nous suggérons également que les entreprises étrangères peuvent atténuer les LOF en tirant stratégiquement parti de la nouveauté de la marque et des plates-formes de marque. Nos analyses empiriques, basées sur un ensemble de données de 257 marques de beauté en Corée du Sud de 2019 à 2022, confirment la présence des LOF dans les innovations de XR, et montrent comment les caractéristiques technologiques et les facteurs spécifiques à la marque influencent l'ampleur des LOF. Nos résultats apportent des renseignements précieux aux entreprises internationales qui élaborent des stratégies visant à configurer des technologies immersives sur les marchés internationaux. Extended reality (XR) technologies, which include augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), are transforming how businesses interact with customers by providing highly immersive and interactive experiences. The global XR market is expanding rapidly and is expected to exceed $250 billion by 2028. However, multinational companies encounter distinct challenges when using XR in foreign markets. These challenges, known as the liability of foreignness (LOF), occur because foreign companies often struggle to deliver XR experiences that are as engaging as those provided by local competitors. This study examines the extent of LOF in XR innovations and identifies key factors affecting its impact. This research examines how effectively XR technologies enhance brand engagement for foreign versus local brands, analyzing 375,477 observations of brand buzz data from 257 beauty brands in South Korea between 2019 and 2022. The researchers also evaluate how the effectiveness of XR technology depends on the XR technology's features as well as brand-specific factors. The study finds that foreign brands experience LOF in XR, meaning their XR efforts are generally less effective in boosting brand engagement compared to local brands. However, the extent of LOF depends on the XR technology's features. Specifically, LOF tends to be greater for XR technologies that are less realistic, more interactive, and more vivid. These features require a deeper understanding of cultural nuances to help customers visualize and engage with XR experiences. Foreign brands can reduce LOF by leveraging their newness, as customers are more inclined to engage with XR from newer brands as a way to resolve uncertainty. Additionally, using communication-centered platforms can help foreign brands build stronger customer relationships and better understand local preferences, reducing LOF. Title: The multinational enterprise, capabilities, and digitalization: governance and growth with world disorder
Abstract: Abstract This essay revisits my 2014 JIBS article about the potential for integrating international business internalization theory with a strategic management capabilities perspective. It recaps the capabilities framework with an emphasis on the learning required of emerging market multinationals and illustrates this with the case of Hyundai Motor Company’s internationalization and growth. It also discusses two aspects of the global economy that have become more prominent since 2014 in shaping international business: geopolitical uncertainty and digitalization. A rise in geopolitical tensions appears to be rebalancing the relationships between multinationals and home/host governments. Digitalization facilitates international business; but it adds new vulnerabilities by (further) accelerating competition, enabling new rivals, and introducing systemic risks into digital supply chains. Implications for managers, board members, and international business scholars are drawn.

How does colonial history matter for expatriate adjustment? The case of Brazilians in Portugal
Authors: Roberta Aguzzoli, Martyna Śliwa, Jorge Lengler, Chris Brewster, Denise Rossato Quatrin
Abstract: Abstract The literature on expatriation typically assumes that cultural and institutional familiarity facilitates expatriate adjustment. This assumption underplays the role of the historical context, especially the influence of painful colonial pasts that often lie beneath such familiarity. In addition, seeking to capture expatriate adjustment as a single measure, such literature does not engage with the differences in the extent to which expatriates achieve cognitive, behavioral, and affective adjustment. Using a qualitative study addressing the work experiences of Brazilians living in Portugal, we argue that to fully understand expatriate adjustment, we must pay attention to the historical colonial relationship between the expatriate’s home and host country. Specifically, we discuss the importance of social representations of history for how expatriates narrate, interpret, and act in response to their experiences. Our research makes two theoretical contributions. First, we explain how historical colonial relationships affect expatriate adjustment and how this leads to adjustment only being partial. Second, we develop a nuanced understanding of expatriate adjustment by drawing attention to its three interdependent dimensions (cognitive, behavioral, and affective), showing that an expatriate may be well adjusted in one dimension but less adjusted in another. We call for organizations to engage more, and more critically, with history.

Title: Worldwide spread of the Weinstein scandal and the #MeToo movement: cross-country diffusion of reputation loss in the film industry
Authors: Fiona Kun Yao, Mingrui Xu, Jiayue Ao
Abstract: Con un enfoque en el contexto moral de la industria cultural, examinamos la perdida de reputación diseminada mundialmente relacionada con el escándalo sexual de Harvey Weinstein en la industria cinematográfica. Específicamente, explora, como el escándalo y el movimiento moral #MeToo relacionada afectan la taquilla de las empresas multinacionales en mercados internacionales. Apalancándose en un enfoque institucional, predecimos que la amplia cobertura de medios tradicionales y digitales del movimiento #MeToo en un país anfitrión promoverá la convergencia de atención y sólidas instituciones formales y no formales de igualdad de género impulsaran la convergencia moral. La atención y la convergencia moral fomentan la propagación entre países de la pérdida de reputación tras el escándalo, penalizando potencialmente a las empresas multinacionales asociadas con The Weinstein Company y afectando negativamente a sus ingresos internacionales. Por el contrario, las diferencias en la cobertura de los medios tradicionales y digitales y el desajuste entre las instituciones formales e informales dificultan la propagación de la pérdida de reputación. Apoyamos nuestras predicciones con datos semanales de ingresos mundiales de taquilla para las empresas multinacionales cinematográficas de 2015 a 2019 en 86 países y una especificación de diferencia en diferencia. Nuestro estudio aporta ideas a la investigación sobre industrias culturales y negocios internacionales, enfatizando el papel de los medios de comunicación masivos y las instituciones en el movimiento moral mundial. Además, analizamos el impacto social de nuestro estudio sobre la igualdad de género. With a focus on the moral context of the cultural industry, we examine the worldwide spread of reputation loss associated with the Harvey Weinstein sex scandal in the film industry. Specifically, we explore how the scandal and the related #MeToo moral movement affect the box office of multinational enterprises (MNEs) in international markets. By leveraging an institutional approach, we predict that extensive traditional and digital media coverage of #MeToo in a host country will promote attention convergence, and robust formal and informal institutions of gender equality will drive moral convergence. Attention and moral convergence foster the cross-country spread of reputation loss following the scandal, potentially penalizing MNEs associated with The Weinstein Company and adversely affecting their international revenue. Conversely, differences in traditional and digital media coverage and misaligned formal and informal institutions hinder the spread of reputation loss. We support our predictions with weekly global box office revenue data for film MNEs from 2015 to 2019 across 86 countries and a difference-in-difference specification. Our study provides insights into research on cultural industries and international business, emphasizing the role of mass media and institutions in the worldwide moral movement. We also discuss the social impact of our study on gender equality. Especificamente, exploramos como o escândalo e o relacionado movimento moral #MeToo afetam bilheterias de empresas multinacionais (MNEs) em mercados internacionais. Usando uma abordagem institucional, prevemos que uma extensa cobertura da mídia tradicional e digital sobre #MeToo em um país anfitrião promoverá a convergência da atenção, e instituições formais e informais robustas de igualdade de gênero impulsionarão uma convergência moral. Title: User language and cultural product innovation: insights from the global mobile gaming industry
Authors: Pengxiang Zhang, Jingtao Yi, Chao Niu, Eric Yanfei Zhao, Sali Li
Abstract: Les recherches traditionnelles sur les industries culturelles ont mis l'accent sur l'innovation localisée, enracinée dans les pays d'origine des produits culturels. Bien que cette recherche reconnaisse l'importance de l'origine de la production, la transformation numérique des industries culturelles a modifié le paysage de l'innovation des produits culturels, passant de processus localisés traditionnels à une approche plus mondialisée et démocratique en impliquant les utilisateurs du monde entier. Cependant, il existe une lacune notable dans la compréhension des variations de la demande chez les utilisateurs de différents pays, d'autant plus que la numérisation permet aux langues des utilisateurs mondiaux de véhiculer des intrants linguistiques divers. Pour combler cette lacune, nous étudions comment la référence temporelle future (Future-Time Reference - FTR) des utilisateurs dans les différents pays influence la vitesse de l'innovation des produits culturels dans l'industrie des jeux mobiles. En analysant un échantillon mondial de 7 787 jeux mobiles, nous constatons que dans les pays où les joueurs utilisent principalement des langues à faible FTR, leur communication présente un cadrage temporel proche, ce qui favorise l'introduction de nouveaux contenus de jeux à une vitesse plus rapide. En outre, l'efficacité de ce cadrage FTR est plus prononcée lorsque les éditeurs prêtent une grande attention aux langues des joueurs ou les connaissent bien. Ces résultats apportent des renseignements importants non seulement à la recherche sur le pays d'origine et les industries culturelles, mais ainsi aux gestionnaires, leur permettant d’impliquer les utilisateurs dans la conduite de l'innovation des produits culturels. 传统的文化产业研究强调文化产品创新受原产国差异影响。虽然原产国的作用很重要，但在数字化转型背景下，文化产品的创新模式已经从原产国为主的模式转向吸引世界各地的用户共同创新的模式。然而，我们对不同国家用户对产品的需求的差异仍然缺乏充分的理解，特别是在全球化的背景下，多样化的语言反馈所带来的影响还有待研究。为填补这一空白，我们研究了跨国用户的未来时间参照（FTR）如何影响移动游戏行业文化产品创新的速度。通过分析全球 7,787 款手机游戏样本， 我们发现， 在游戏玩家主要使用弱 FTR 语言的国家中， 他们的交流呈现出更贴近当下的时间框架， 从而促使新游戏内容以更快的速度推出。此外， 当游戏发行商密切关注或熟悉游戏玩家的语言时， 这种 FTR 框架的有效性就会变得更加明显。这些发现为原产国效应和文化产业的研究提供了重要见解，也为管理者更好地吸引用户推动文化产品创新提供了参考。 Traditional studies on cultural industries have emphasized localized innovation rooted in cultural products’ countries of origin. While this research acknowledges the significance of production origin, the digital transformation of cultural industries has shifted the landscape of cultural product innovation from traditional localized processes to a more globalized and democratic approach by engaging users worldwide. However, there is a notable gap in understanding demand-side variations in users from different countries, particularly as digitalization allows global users’ languages to convey diverse linguistic inputs. To address this gap, we investigate how users’ future-time reference (FTR) across countries influences the pace of cultural product innovation in the mobile gaming industry. Analyzing a global sample of 7787 mobile games, we find that in countries where gamers predominantly use weak FTR languages, their communication exhibits proximate temporal framing, prompting the introduction of new gaming content at a faster pace. Further, the effectiveness of such FTR framing becomes more pronounced when publishers pay close attention to or are familiar with gamers’ languages. These findings contribute important insights for research on country of origin and cultural industries and for managers to better engage users to drive cultural product innovation. Title: The liability of gender? Constraints and enablers of foreign market entry for female artists
Authors: JungYun Han, Henrich R. Greve, Andrew Shipilov
Abstract: Les industries culturelles contribuent à bâtir des économies fondées sur la créativité et à stimuler les échanges culturels à l’échelle mondiale, mais ce processus se heurte à des contraintes. L’une de ces contraintes réside dans le traitement inégal entre les sexes. Lorsque des artistes féminines exportent des produits culturels, elles sont confrontées à des handicaps liés au genre ( Liability of Gender ), définis comme des difficultés spécifiques au genre pour surmonter les handicaps et coûts liés au statut étranger de l’individu ou de l’organisation ( Liability of Foreignness ). Les attentes sexospécifiques du public et le manque d’informations des artistes sur les marchés étrangers réduiront la probabilité des femmes artistes de réussir l’exportation de leurs produits culturels par rapport à leurs homologues masculins. Les différences en matière d’éducation et de connexions aux réseaux sociaux renforcent cet impact. Afin d’examiner cette relation et de découvrir comment elle peut être contrebalancée, nous étudions les artistes coréens durant la période 2000 - 2015. Nous démontrons que les artistes féminines ont plus de difficultés à exposer dans des galeries étrangères que les hommes, mais ces impacts négatifs peuvent être atténués par l'éducation d'élite et par la participation à des programmes de résidence artistique. Ces derniers aident les femmes artistes à développer des réseaux à partir de leurs interactions avec leurs pairs féminines, mais ces bénéfices s'érodent rapidement par rapport à ceux liés à l'éducation. Ces résultats nous aident à comprendre comment créer des règles du jeu équitables entre les sexes dans les échanges culturels mondiaux, et suggèrent que les institutions de création de réseaux telles que les programmes de résidence artistique peuvent réduire efficacement les inégalités entre les sexes. Las industrias culturales ayudan a construir economías basadas en la creatividad y estimulan los intercambios culturales a lo largo del mundo, pero este proceso enfrenta restricciones. Una de estas restricciones el trato desigual de los géneros. Cuando las artistas mujeres exportan productos culturales enfrentan “desventajas de género”, definido como las dificultades especificas asociadas al género para superar las desventajas de extranjería. Tanto las expectativas de género del público como la falta de información de las artistas sobre los mercados extranjeros van a disminuir las probabilidades de las mujeres para exportar sus productos de manera exitosa en comparación con sus homólogos hombres. Para investigar esta relación y descubrir cómo puede contrarrestarse, estudiamos a artistas coreanas de 2000 a 2015. Documentamos que las mujeres artistas tienen más dificultades para exponer en galerías extranjeras que los hombres, aunque estos efectos negativos pueden mitigarse mediante una educación de élite y la participación en programas de residencia artística. Los programas de residencia ayudan a las mujeres artistas a desarrollar redes a partir de sus interacciones con compañeras, pero estos beneficios se erosionan rápidamente en relación con los beneficios de la educación. Estas conclusiones nos ayudan a comprender cómo crear igualdad de condiciones entre los géneros en los intercambios culturales mundiales y sugieren que las instituciones que crean redes, como los programas de residencias artísticas, pueden reducir eficazmente la desigualdad de género. In particular, we focus on female artists' “double liability”—both as foreigners and as women—when trying to penetrate foreign markets. The research was carried out on fine art professionals in South Korea, a market predominantly controlled by male artists. Corruption experience and foreign investments: clean hands or dirty hands learning?
Authors: Negash Haile Dedho, René Belderbos, Alvaro Cuervo-Cazurra
Abstract: Corruption, defined as the misuse of power for personal gain, affects multinational corporations (MNCs) in complex ways. It increases costs and uncertainties but can also help firms bypass inefficient regulations. While corruption generally discourages investment, some firms still invest in corrupt countries to take advantage of opportunities there, leveraging their experience with corruption elsewhere. This study explores how MNCs learn from corrupt environments and how this learning influences their investment decisions. It distinguishes between “clean hands learning,” where firms avoid bribery, and “dirty hands learning,” where they engage in bribery but conceal it. The study examines how home-country laws against bribery abroad impact these learning types. This article investigates the investment choices of 25,067 MNCs from 97 countries, focusing on 91,371 greenfield investments (new ventures in foreign countries) made between 2008 and 2016. The researchers used data from the Financial Times’ fDi Markets database and other sources to analyze how corruption in host countries affects MNCs’ investment decisions. They considered the role of home-country enforcement of anti-bribery laws and how MNCs’ prior experiences in corrupt countries influence their decisions, and used statistical models to assess the impact of these factors on investment choices. The results show that corruption generally deters MNCs from investing in a country. However, firms with experience in corrupt environments are less discouraged by corruption when making new investments. Home-country enforcement of anti-bribery laws strengthens the deterrent effect of corruption, especially for firms with corruption experience (“dirty hands learning”). This suggests that such enforcement effectively reduces unethical behavior by making firms more cautious about investing in corrupt countries. The study highlights the importance of international anti-bribery laws and suggests that stronger enforcement can curb unethical practices by MNCs. Future research could explore direct measures of clean and dirty hands learning to better understand how firms navigate corruption in global markets. Para enfrentar los desafíos de operar en un país anfitrión corrupto, pueden utilizar la experiencia adquirida en otros países corruptos. Distinguimos entre el aprendizaje de ”manos limpias” y “manos sucias” sobre la corrupción, es decir, aprender cómo evitar el soborno, o aprender cómo pagar sobornos y evitar la trazabilidad. Title: Prosocial motivation and lending to the poor: evidence from an international crowdfunding platform
Authors: Luqun Xie, Yi Ding, Jiatao Li, Haifeng Xu
Abstract: Employing a prosocial perspective, this study examines how crowdfunders' prosocial motivation influences their lending decisions on international crowdfunding platforms, addressing the global challenge of poverty alleviation. We posit that prosocially motivated crowdfunders, concerned about economic inequality and others' well-being, are more likely to lend to poorer borrowers to minimize inequality and improve welfare. Analyzing a large dataset from Kiva.org with machine learning techniques, we find that higher prosocial motivation indeed leads to the lending choice of poorer borrowers across borders. However, cultural distance weakens this relationship by creating cognitive and emotional barriers, while crowdfunders' platform experience and women-owned businesses strengthen it. These findings highlight how digital platforms enable prosocial motivations to cross national borders in poverty-reduction efforts, while revealing barriers and enablers in cross-border lending. Our study contributes to the international business literature by introducing a prosocial perspective to digital platform research and advancing methodological approaches through machine learning. For practitioners, we suggest strategies to enhance prosocial crowdfunding platforms' effectiveness, including cultural bridge-building initiatives, leveraging experienced users as mentors, and highlighting women-owned businesses. Policymakers can use these insights to create frameworks maximizing prosocial crowdfunding's impact on poverty alleviation. In recent years, the rise of digital platforms has opened up new possibilities for addressing global challenges like poverty. One innovative approach is through prosocial (intended to benefit others) crowdfunding platforms like Kiva, which allow people to lend money to entrepreneurs in developing countries without requiring collateral (assets pledged by a borrower to secure a loan) or charging interest. However, there's a gap in understanding how the motivations of these crowdfunders influence their decisions to lend across national borders. This study delves into the prosocial motivations of crowdfunders and how factors like cultural distance, experience, and the gender of business owners affect their lending choices. This study analyzed data from Kiva.org, the largest international prosocial crowdfunding platform. The researchers used machine learning (a type of artificial intelligence that allows computers to learn from data) techniques to assess the prosocial motivation of crowdfunders based on their self-reported reasons for joining Kiva. The study focused on transactions from 2010 to 2019, involving crowdfunders from five major countries and loans to borrowers across 28 countries. The key research question was whether crowdfunders with a higher prosocial motivation are more likely to support poorer borrowers, and how cultural distance, crowdfunder experience, and women-owned businesses might moderate this relationship. The results showed that crowdfunders with a strong prosocial motivation – defined as the desire to benefit others – are indeed more likely to lend to poorer borrowers. However, cultural distance (differences in social norms and languages) can weaken this effect, making it harder for crowdfunders to empathize with and understand borrowers from very different backgrounds. On the other hand, crowdfunders with more experience on the platform are better at overcoming these barriers, and loans for women-owned businesses tend to attract more support from prosocially motivated crowdfunders. The study concludes that while digital platforms can bridge the gap between lenders and borrowers worldwide, cultural differences still pose a challenge. However, experienced crowdfunders and a focus on women-owned businesses can enhance the impact of prosocial lending. Title: MNEs and financing climate change transitions: the challenge of collective action
Abstract: This article discusses the role of multinational enterprises (MNEs) in addressing climate change. MNEs are large companies that operate in multiple countries. The authors argue that MNEs have a unique position to help tackle climate change because of their global reach and resources. They highlight that MNEs can lead efforts in financing climate initiatives, spreading technology, and influencing regulations. However, the authors also note that MNEs face challenges, such as balancing financial performance with environmental responsibilities and dealing with different regulations across countries. This article explores how MNEs can contribute to solving climate change issues. The authors suggest that MNEs can use their international operations to manage resources efficiently and spread green technologies. They emphasize the importance of corporate governance (the system by which companies are directed and controlled) in promoting environmental responsibility. The authors also discuss financial innovations, like linking debt costs to carbon emissions, as ways to encourage MNEs to reduce their environmental impact. They acknowledge the pressure on executives from stakeholders (people or groups affected by the company’s actions) to act on climate issues. The authors recommend partnerships between MNEs and other organizations to address these challenges. The authors conclude that MNEs have significant potential to influence global climate change efforts positively. They highlight the importance of MNEs’ governance systems in supporting these initiatives. However, they also point out the difficulties MNEs face, such as navigating different legal systems and managing diverse stakeholder expectations. The article suggests that while MNEs can play a crucial role, they cannot do it alone and need collaboration with governments and other entities. In the future, MNEs could drive more sustainable practices worldwide if they overcome these challenges and align their strategies with global climate goals. Reconociendo que este papel es complejo y multifacético, prestan especial atención al financiamiento de iniciativas contra el cambio climático y las ventajas únicas que tienen las empresas multinacionales en este aspecto. Reflexiono sobre los argumentos y propuestas clave de Allen et al. y sus supuestos subyacentes, que encontré excesivamente optimistas en múltiples aspectos. El denominador común en la gama de cuestiones y preguntas que planteo es el desafío de coordinar la acción colectiva—ya sea entre estados nación, empresas multinacionales, ONG o alguna combinación de estos—en lo que es inherentemente un tema de escala global. Concluyo delineando una agenda de investigación futura. Allen et al. (2024a) present an insightful and comprehensive analysis of the role multinationals (MNEs) can play in tackling worldwide climate change challenges. Acknowledging that this role is complex and multifaceted, they pay special attention to the financing of climate change initiatives and the unique advantages MNEs have in this regard. I reflect on Allen et al.’s key arguments and proposals and their underlying assumptions, which I found to be overly optimistic on multiple grounds. The common denominator in the range of issues and questions I raise is the challenge of coordinating collective action – either among nation-states, MNEs, NGOs, or some combination thereof – on what is inherently a global-scale issue. I conclude by outlining a future research agenda.
